macau: Macau lies on China's southern coast, 60 km west of Hong Kong, on the south shore of Zhongshan Island on the western side of the Pearl River estuary. It consists of the Macau Peninsula, Taipa, Coloane and the Cotai reclamation zone between them. The peninsula was originally a separate island with hilly terrain that became a tombolo as a sandbar formed, and natural sedimentation and land reclamation have enlarged it. The land area grew from 10.28 square kilometres in the late 19th century to 32.9 square kilometres in 2018.

During the Qin dynasty (221–206 BCE) the region came under Panyu County, Nanhai Commandery, and it is first known to have been settled in the Han dynasty. In 1152, under the Song, it fell under the new Xiangshan County. In 1277 about 50,000 refugees fleeing the Mongol conquest of China settled on the coast. The earliest written record of the name, A Ma Gang, is in a letter of 20 November 1555. It refers to the sea goddess Matsu, or A-Ma, whose temple the local people took the Portuguese to be asking about when they gave the name Ma Kok.

The explorer Jorge Álvares, the first European to reach China by sea, arrived in 1513. Portuguese merchants set up a trading post at Tamão, now Tuen Mun, but after their expulsion in 1521 the Ming and Portuguese navies clashed. Portugal lost two ships at the Battle of Tamão in 1521 and two more at the Battle of Sincouwaan; later defeats came at Shuangyu in 1548 and near Dongshan County in 1549. Merchants kept trying to settle on the Pearl River estuary and finally settled at Macau.

The Ming dynasty first leased the territory to Portugal as a trading post in 1557. Portugal paid an annual rent and administered it under Chinese sovereignty until 1887, when the Sino-Portuguese Treaty of Peking gave it perpetual colonial rights. Portuguese rule lasted until the handover to China in 1999. The Sino-Portuguese Joint Declaration provided for economic and administrative continuity, and the Basic Law of Macao, under the principle of one country, two systems, serves as the regional constitution.

Macau is a special administrative region of China, with a population of about 720,000 and one of the highest densities in the world. Its economy rests largely on casino gaming and tourism. More than four centuries of Chinese and Portuguese contact have left a mixed culture, with Macanese people of mixed Portuguese ancestry, and a downtown that blends Portuguese, French, English, Italian and Chinese architecture. The historic centre was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
machu-picchu: Machu Picchu stands in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru, on a narrow saddle between two peaks, Machu Picchu and Huayna Picchu, at about 2,430 metres. It lies some 80 kilometres north-west of Cusco and more than 1,000 metres lower than the Inca capital, so its climate was milder. The Urubamba River bends round the site on three sides, and cliffs drop 450 metres to the water. A study of 2021 suggests that its builders called it Huayna Picchu, or simply Picchu.

The dating is debated. Models based on John H. Rowe's reconstruction of the reign of Pachacuti put the start of building around 1450, while radiocarbon measurements on human remains, reported in a 2021 study led by Richard L. Burger, indicate occupation from about 1420 to 1530. Archaeologists generally hold that Pachacuti ordered the royal estate after conquering the middle and lower Urubamba, as part of a programme of royal estates along the river, though no contemporary written record confirms it.

The estate seems to have been a seasonal retreat. About 750 people are estimated to have lived there, most of them permanent support staff known as yanaconas, with religious specialists and temporary workers. The site was abandoned in the mid-16th century, around the time of the Spanish conquest, probably because Inca rule collapsed and disease followed European contact; smallpox may have killed most of its inhabitants before the conquistadors arrived.

The forest overgrew the ruins, and few outside the area knew of them. The Peruvian explorer Agustín Lizárraga reached the site in the early 20th century, but the American historian Hiram Bingham III brought it to international attention in 1911.

The citadel is built in the classical Inca style, with finely worked dry-stone walls. About 200 buildings stand on parallel terraces round a central square, divided into an agricultural sector and an urban sector with an upper and a lower town. Its main structures include the Temple of the Sun, the Temple of the Three Windows and the Intihuatana stone. Peru declared a Historic Sanctuary there in 1981, and UNESCO listed Machu Picchu as a World Heritage Site in 1983.
madagascar: Madagascar covers 592,800 square kilometres and is the world's fourth-largest island and second-largest island country. It split from Africa around 180 million years ago and from the Indian subcontinent approximately 90 million years ago, so that its plants and animals evolved in relative isolation; over 90 per cent of its wildlife is endemic. A narrow, steep escarpment with tropical lowland forest runs along the east coast, and west of it lies a central plateau of terraced, rice-growing valleys between 750 and 1,500 metres high. The highest point is Maromokotro, at 2,876 metres.

Madagascar was first permanently settled during or before the mid-first millennium CE by Austronesian peoples, presumably arriving by outrigger canoe from present-day Indonesia, and scholars are cautious about dates earlier than 250 CE. The first settlers met giant lemurs, elephant birds and Malagasy hippopotamuses, which later became extinct through hunting and habitat destruction. Arab traders reached the island between the 7th and 9th centuries and brought Islam and the Arabic script, adapted as sorabe. Bantu-speaking migrants from south-eastern Africa arrived around the year 1000, and zebu cattle from South India were brought about then.

Until the late 18th century a fragmented set of shifting alliances ruled the island. King Andrianjaka founded Antananarivo as capital of the Imerina Kingdom around 1610 or 1625. From the early 19th century a series of Merina nobles united most of the island as the Kingdom of Madagascar. France's annexation ended the monarchy, and the country became independent in 1960.

Madagascar has had four republics and has been a constitutional democracy since 1992. A political crisis and coup in 2009 led to a long transition, and constitutional governance returned in January 2014. Malagasy and French are the official languages.

The Malagasy form over 90 per cent of the population, divided into 18 ethnic subgroups, of which the Merina of the highlands are the largest at about 26 per cent. The Malagasy language is of Malayo-Polynesian origin, closest to Ma'anyan of Borneo. The valiha, the most emblematic instrument, is a bamboo tube zither carried by early settlers from southern Borneo.
madeira: Madeira lies in the North Atlantic, in the region of Macaronesia, just under 400 kilometres north of the Canary Islands, 520 kilometres west of Morocco and 805 kilometres south-west of mainland Portugal. The archipelago includes the islands of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas, administered together with the separate Savage Islands. The main island is mountainous, with Pico Ruivo reaching 1,862 metres. It is wet in the north-west and dry in the south-east. The Portuguese name means wood, after the forest that once covered the island; settlers burned much of it to clear land, though laurel forests survive on the northern slopes. From the 16th century the settlers built levadas, irrigation channels carrying water to the dry south.

Ancient authors and legend hint at earlier knowledge of the islands. Plutarch, in his life of Sertorius, reports sailors' tales of two Atlantic islands called the Isles of the Blessed, and archaeological evidence suggests the Vikings may have visited between 900 and 1030. A legend of the lovers Robert Machim and Anna d'Arfet, driven ashore in 1346, is said to have given Machico its name. Medieval atlases such as the Medici-Laurentian Atlas of 1351 show the islands. The uninhabited archipelago was claimed in 1419 by Portuguese sailors in the service of Prince Henry the Navigator and settled after 1420.

Sicilian advisers and Genoese capital transformed its sugar industry, with water-driven mills and the levadas, and by 1490 Madeira was the principal source of European sugar. The sugar was cultivated by enslaved labour. In the 18th century vineyards replaced the sugar plantations, in a wine trade dominated by English merchants, and British forces first occupied the island in 1801. On 3 December 1916 the German submarine SM U-38 sank three ships in Funchal harbour and bombarded the city. In April 1931 the garrison joined a military uprising against the National Dictatorship, crushed by mainland forces after seven days. After the 1974 Carnation Revolution a separatist front carried out about 200 bomb attacks before the 1976 Constitution granted Madeira its own administration and legislature.

Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal and an outermost region of the European Union. Its capital and largest city is Funchal, on the south coast of the main island, and about half the population lives there. The population was 251,060 in 2021, mostly descended from Portuguese settlers. Madeira wine, a fortified wine, goes back to the Age of Exploration, when the islands were a standard port of call for ships bound for the New World and the East Indies. Its laurel forest is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
madhya-pradesh: Madhya Pradesh, whose name means Central Province, lies in the geographic heart of India. It borders Rajasthan to the northwest, Uttar Pradesh to the northeast, Chhattisgarh to the east, Maharashtra to the south and Gujarat to the west. The state straddles the Narmada River, which runs east and west between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges; these ranges and the river are the traditional boundary between the north and south of India. The Narmada is considered very sacred and is worshipped throughout the region, and the Tapti runs parallel to it. The highest point is Dhupgarh, at 1,350 m.

Isolated remains of Homo erectus found at Hathnora in the Narmada Valley suggest the area may have been inhabited in the Middle Pleistocene. Painted pottery of the later Mesolithic period has been found in the Bhimbetka rock shelters, and Chalcolithic sites of the Kayatha culture (2100-1800 BCE) and the Malwa culture (1700-1500 BCE) lie in the west. The region includes the area of the ancient Avanti Mahajanapada, whose capital Ujjain arose as a major city in the sixth century BCE.

Major dynasties of India ruled the region in later centuries, and the Maratha Empire dominated most of it in the 18th century. After the Third Anglo-Maratha War it was divided into several princely states under the British. After independence, the Central Provinces and Berar was renamed Madhya Pradesh, with Nagpur as its capital, and the Central India Agency became Madhya Bharat, with Gwalior as its capital. In 1956 these states were reorganised and combined with Vindhya Pradesh and Bhopal into the new Madhya Pradesh. The state was the largest in India by area until 2000, when its southeastern Chhattisgarh region became a separate state.

Bhopal is the capital, and other major cities include Indore, Gwalior, Jabalpur and Sagar. The state has over 72 million residents, and Hindi is its official language. Tribal groups such as the Gondi, Bhil, Baiga and Korku form a significant part of the population. UNESCO has declared three sites in the state World Heritage Sites: the Khajuraho Group of Monuments (1986), the Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi (1989) and the Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka (2003). Buddhism and Jainism were once prominent here, especially on the central plateau near Raisen and Bhopal, and Malwa still has a significant Jain minority.
madrid: Madrid lies in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula on the southern Meseta Central, 60 kilometres south of the Guadarrama mountain range, at an average altitude of about 650 metres. It straddles the Jarama and Manzanares river sub-drainage basins, within the wider catchment of the Tagus. The oldest urban core stands on hills beside the left bank of the Manzanares. The city grew eastwards to the creek now followed by the Paseo de la Castellana and on to the Abroñigal Creek, and also by annexing neighbouring settlements.

The origin of the name is unknown. Theories include a Latin derivation from matrix, a Celtic form meaning 'ford', and an Arabic word for a water stream, majrā. All have difficulty explaining the phonetic change fully. Nicknames include Los Madriles and La Villa y Corte, 'the town and court'.

The site has been occupied since prehistoric times. Archaeological remains include a settlement of the Celtic Carpetani, Roman villas, a Visigoth basilica near the church of Santa María de la Almudena and three Visigoth necropolises. The first historical document of an established settlement dates from the Muslim period. In the second half of the 9th century the Umayyad emir Muhammad I built a fortress on a headland near the Manzanares, one of many on the border between Al-Andalus and the kingdoms of León and Castile, to protect Toledo from attack from the north.

After the Caliphate of Córdoba broke up in the early 11th century, Madrid became part of the Taifa of Toledo. In 1083 Alfonso VI of León and Castile seized it as an outpost against Toledo, which he took in 1085. Christians then occupied the centre of the town, while Muslims and Jews were displaced to the suburbs. Madrid remained a borderland for a time and suffered raids during the Almoravid period; its walls were destroyed in 1110. Philip II moved his court to Madrid in 1561 and transformed the town into a capital city.

Madrid is the capital and largest city of Spain and of the autonomous community of Madrid, with about 3.4 million people in the city proper. Its landmarks include the Plaza Mayor, built in 1617 to 1619 and attributed to Juan Gómez de Mora, the Royal Palace, the Buen Retiro Park, founded in 1631, and the Prado, Reina Sofía and Thyssen-Bornemisza museums along the Paseo del Prado, which form a UNESCO World Heritage site called the Golden Triangle of Art.
maeotians: The name comes from the sea: Maeotian was at first a label for the tribes living around the Maeotis, above all on its eastern coast. In sources of the 4th century BCE it has three senses: a broad term for the peoples around the sea, the name of the coastal tribes later listed by Strabo, and, in the usage of the Bosporan chancery, the lesser tribes of the Kuban region as distinct from the Sindi.

Their language, and even its family, is uncertain; the place names of their country suggest that they were not of Iranian stock. The Cambridge Ancient History reports two main views, that they were of Cimmerian ancestry, akin to the Thracians, or that they were Caucasian natives under Iranian overlordship. Soviet scholars concluded that they were among the ancestors of the Circassian, or Adyghe, people.

Strabo names among them the Sindi, Dandarii, Toreatae, Agri, Arrechi, Tarpetes, Obidiaceni, Sittaceni and Dosci, and adds that there were many others. Which peoples counted as Maeotian was disputed already in antiquity: Hellanicus of Lesbos and Pseudo-Scylax set the Sindi apart, while Pseudo-Scymnus and Strabo include them. The Sindi are the best attested and were probably the dominant people of the region.

The Maeotians lived in earthworks and open settlements on the Taman Peninsula and along the middle Kuban. According to Strabo they were as warlike as their nomadic neighbours, paid tribute at times to the rulers of Tanais and at times to the Bosporans, and rose in revolt from time to time. In the Kuban region they lived under successive steppe overlords. The graves show it: the ruling Scythians, and in Sindica the Sindian elite, were buried in richly furnished kurgans, while the Maeotian population used poorly equipped flat cemeteries.

In the early 4th century BCE Maeotian tribes fought a major war against the Bosporan Kingdom and its Sindian subjects. When the Sindian king Hecataeus repudiated his Maeotian wife Tirgatao, she roused her people, the Ixomatae, and other tribes to a destructive war on both kingdoms, which ended only under Gorgippus through supplication and gifts.

After Leucon I annexed Sindica, probably in the 380s BCE, the tribes of the Kuban were brought into the Bosporan state by stages. Leucon ruled the Toretae, Dandarii and Psessi as king, and under Paerisades I the royal style became king of the Sindi and all the Maeotians. Under Aspurgus, in the early 1st century CE, the royal titles still listed the Sindi and Maeotians, now with the Tarpetes and the people of Tanais.
magdeburg: Magdeburg stands on the Elbe river and is the capital of the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. It is first mentioned in a document as Magadoburg in the Capitulary of Diedenhofen issued by Charlemagne in 805, and the name probably comes from Old High German magado, big or mighty, and burg, fortress. The city marked its 1,200th anniversary in 2005.

King Henry the Fowler fortified the town in 919 against the Magyars and Slavs. In 929 King Otto I granted it to his English-born wife Edith as dower, and Otto himself was buried in the cathedral. The archbishops played a prominent part in the German colonisation of the Slavic lands east of the Elbe. In 1035 the city received a patent giving it the right to hold trade exhibitions, which formed the basis of the Magdeburg rights. In the thirteenth century Magdeburg joined the Hanseatic League. Fires in 1188 and 1207 destroyed much of it.

Martin Luther preached there in 1524, after which the city left Roman Catholicism, and Matthias Flacius and his companions wrote the Magdeburg Centuries there. The city withstood a siege by Albrecht von Wallenstein in 1629. In 1631 imperial troops under Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, stormed it, massacred the inhabitants and burned it, and only about 4,000 people remained after the war. Otto von Guericke, its mayor and a scientist, led the recovery. Under the Peace of Westphalia the city passed to Brandenburg-Prussia in 1680.

Magdeburg surrendered to French troops in 1806 and in 1815 became the capital of the Prussian Province of Saxony. A British air raid on 16 January 1945 destroyed much of the city centre. It belonged to East Germany from 1949 to 1990, and in 1990 became the capital of Saxony-Anhalt.
magnetic-compass: Early references to lodestone and its attraction of iron come from several cultures. The Greek philosopher Thales of Miletus, in the 6th century BCE, was credited with discovering that a lodestone attracts iron, and the Sushruta Samhita, an ancient Indian medical text, describes using it to remove arrows from a body. The earliest Chinese literary reference to magnetism is in the 4th-century BCE Guiguzi, and the Lüshi Chunqiu of the 2nd century BCE states that the lodestone makes iron come to it. The Lunheng, composed between 20 and 100 CE, says that a lodestone attracts a needle.

The first devices to use these properties may date to Han China. In the 2nd century BCE Chinese geomancers were experimenting with a south-pointing spoon of lodestone for divination, which turns to a north–south axis on a smooth bronze plate, though archaeologists have not found a magnetite spoon in a Han tomb. Some historians believe that a compass using an iron fish floating in a vessel of oil was in use in southern India in the 4th century, while others think the evidence for compasses before the 11th century is very weak.

The first compasses used for navigation appeared in China by 1088, under the Song dynasty, as described by Shen Kuo. They were made of iron needles magnetised by striking them with a lodestone. The first use recorded in Western Europe dates to around 1190 and in the Islamic world to the 13th century. Such needles, set in a cork or a piece of wood and floated in a bowl of water, were universally used until the box-like compass with a dry pivoting needle appeared around 1300. The dry compass was supplanted in the early 20th century by the liquid-filled compass.

Compass cards were originally marked only with north or with the four cardinal points. These were later divided into 24 points in China and 32 in Europe, and in the modern era the 360-degree system took hold. Mariners also learned that a compass needle does not point exactly to true north: variation values for most of the oceans had been calculated and published by 1914. Iron in a ship causes further error, called deviation, and navigators made correction tables by comparing compass bearings with landmarks of known magnetic bearing.

A magnetic compass has a magnetised needle that aligns itself with the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field and so points approximately to the north magnetic pole. The needle turns on a low-friction pivot, in better compasses a jewel bearing. The angle between true north and magnetic north is called magnetic declination, and it varies widely from place to place and changes slowly over time. The compass is counted among the Four Great Inventions of China.
mahabharata: Tradition ascribes the Mahabharata to the sage Vyasa, who is also a major figure in the epic and who described it as itihasa, history. Scholars regard the story of the scribe Ganesha writing down Vyasa's dictation as a later interpolation, and the Critical Edition does not include it. The epic began as an orally transmitted tale of charioteer bards. Unlike the Vedas, which had to be preserved letter-perfect, it was a popular work whose reciters conformed to changes in language and style, so its earliest surviving components are believed to be no older than the earliest external references to it, among them Panini's grammar of the 4th century BCE. The text probably reached its final form by the early Gupta period.

The core story is a dynastic struggle for the throne of Hastinapura, ruled by the Kuru clan, between two collateral branches, the Kauravas and the Pandavas. The eldest Kaurava, Duryodhana, is younger than the eldest Pandava, Yudhishthira, and both claim to be first in line. The Pandavas build the capital of Indraprastha, but Duryodhana's uncle Shakuni wins their wealth and kingdom from Yudhishthira with loaded dice. They spend thirteen years in exile, and when negotiations through Krishna fail, both sides summon vast armies to Kurukshetra.

The epic runs to over 100,000 shlokas, about 1.8 million words, roughly ten times the length of the Iliad and the Odyssey combined. It is divided into 18 parvas and holds many other stories, including those of Damayanti, Shakuntala and Savitri and Satyavan, as well as discussions of philosophy and of dharmayuddha, just war, which sets criteria such as proportionality, just means and fair treatment of captives and the wounded. Its best-known part, the Bhagavad Gita, is a dialogue between the Pandava prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna.

Within the Indian tradition the Mahabharata is sometimes called the fifth Veda. Between 1919 and 1966 scholars at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune compared manuscripts from India and abroad and produced the Critical Edition, in 19 volumes on 13,000 pages, which is the text usually used in current studies. The epic was translated into Tamil and Javanese, where part of a Kawi prose version survives from the late 10th century. It inspired plays by Bhasa and many later works, and in the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand villagers still perform the Pandav Lila, a ritual re-enactment of episodes from it. Swami Vivekananda, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Mahatma Gandhi, among others, drew on the text in the Indian independence movement.
mahapadma-nanda: What is told of Mahapadma comes from the Puranas, which make him the first Nanda king and the son of Mahanandin, the last king of the preceding Shaishunaga line, by a Shudra woman. His name, also given as Mahapadma-pati, means lord of the great lotus. Other traditions about the founder of the dynasty do not use this name at all.

Buddhist texts call the first Nanda king Ugrasena and describe him as of unknown lineage. According to the Mahavamsa-tika he came from the frontier region, was captured by a gang of robbers and later became their leader. One theory holds that Ugrasena was probably another name for Mahapadma. Jain texts such as the Parishishtaparvan and the Avashyaka sutra say that the Nanda king was the son of a courtesan by a barber and that he succeeded Udayin, with Kalpaka, a Jain, as his chief minister.

The Puranas describe him as ekarat, sole sovereign, and as sarva-kshatrantaka, destroyer of all the Kshatriyas, the warriors and rulers. The lines he is said to have exterminated include the Maithalas, Kasheyas, Ikshvakus, Panchalas, Shurasenas, Kurus, Haihayas, Vitihotras, Kalingas and Ashmakas.

The length of his reign is uncertain. The Matsya Purana assigns him 88 years, the Vayu Purana only 28. Modern estimates of his coronation also differ: the Indologist F. E. Pargiter put it in 382 BCE, the historian R. K. Mukherjee in 364 BCE and the historian H. C. Raychaudhuri about 345 BCE, and the beginning of Nanda rule has been placed as early as the 5th century BCE.

According to the Puranas, eight sons of Mahapadma ruled in succession after him for twelve years in all; only one, Sukalpa, is named. The Buddhist texts instead make the next eight kings brothers of the first, give the dynasty 22 years in total and name the last of them as Dhana Nanda.

Greek and Roman writers call the Nanda king of the time of Alexander's invasion Agrammes, possibly a corruption of the Sanskrit Augraseniya, son or descendant of Ugrasena. They suggest that the founder was a barber who took the throne from the last king of the earlier dynasty. The Roman historian Curtius, of the 1st century CE, reports on the authority of Porus that this barber became the queen's lover, murdered the king, seized power while pretending to act as guardian of the princes and later killed them, and that the king reigning in Alexander's day was his son.
maharashtra: Maharashtra covers 307,713 square kilometres of the western peninsular region of India and occupies a substantial part of the Deccan Plateau. It has a coastline of 840 kilometres on the Arabian Sea. The dominant feature is the plateau, separated from the narrow Konkan coastal plains by the Western Ghats, also called the Sahyadri Range, which run parallel to the coast and average 1,200 metres in height. The Satpura Hills form its northern border. The Godavari and Krishna are its two major rivers. Its main regions are North Maharashtra, Konkan, Marathwada, Vidarbha and Desh, or Western Maharashtra.

The region has a history of many thousands of years. Late Harappan or Chalcolithic sites of the Jorwe culture, c. 1300 to 700 BCE, have been found throughout the state, the largest at Daimabad, which had a mud fortification and an elliptical temple with fire pits. In the Late Harappan period many people migrated from Gujarat to northern Maharashtra. Among the dynasties that ruled the region were the Asmakas, the Mauryas, the Western Satraps, the Abhiras, the Vakatakas, the Chalukyas, the Western Chalukyas, the Khaljis, the Tughlaqs, the Bahamanis and the Mughals, besides the Satavahanas, Rashtrakutas and Seuna Yadavas.

In the early 19th century the region was divided between the Peshwa's dominions in the Maratha Confederacy and the Nizamate of Hyderabad. The British East India Company then defeated the Marathas and brought most of present-day Maharashtra under its control, directly and through many princely states, and from 1858 the British crown took over. The region was divided among the Bombay Presidency, the Central Provinces, Berar and princely states including Hyderabad. After independence in 1947 the Bombay Presidency became Bombay State, which gained Berar, the Deccan states and the Gujarat states between 1950 and 1956. The United Maharashtra Movement campaigned for a separate state for Marathi speakers, and on 1 May 1960 Bombay State was divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat.

Mumbai is the capital of Maharashtra, with Nagpur as its winter capital, and the state has 36 districts in six divisions. Marathi, written in the Devanagari script, is the official language and is spoken by about 69 per cent of the people. Its earliest literature is the Dnyaneshwari, a commentary on the Bhagavad Gita by the 13th-century Bhakti saint Dnyaneshwar. Seven UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the state, among them the Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta Caves and the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus.
mahatma-gandhi: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 in Porbandar, a coastal town on the Kathiawar Peninsula and then part of a small princely state. His father Karamchand Uttamchand Gandhi was the dewan, or chief minister, of Porbandar and later of Rajkot. A family friend advised that he study law in London, and to win his mother's consent he vowed to abstain from meat, alcohol and women. The elders of the Modh Bania community excommunicated him from his caste, but he sailed on 4 September 1888 and was called to the bar at 22.

After two uncertain years in India, Gandhi went to South Africa in April 1893 to represent an Indian merchant in a lawsuit, and stayed for 21 years. He faced discrimination at once: he was thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg for refusing to leave the first-class compartment. He had thought of himself as a Briton first and an Indian second, but the prejudice he saw made him question his people's standing in the British Empire. There he first used nonviolent resistance, in a campaign for civil rights.

Gandhi returned to India in 1915 at the request of Gopal Krishna Gokhale. He took leadership of the Indian National Congress in 1920 and formulated satyagraha as a political movement in a Resolution on Non-cooperation that September. Congress declared the independence of India on 26 January 1930, and that year he led the 400 km Dandi Salt March against the British salt tax. In 1942 he demanded immediate independence, and the British imprisoned him and tens of thousands of Congress leaders. He was imprisoned many times in both South Africa and India.

The Muslim League moved, against Gandhi's strong opposition, to demand a separate Muslim state. In August 1947 the British partitioned the land, and India and Pakistan each became independent on terms Gandhi disapproved. Religious violence followed, especially in Punjab and Bengal. He visited the affected areas and undertook several hunger strikes to stop the violence.

On 30 January 1948 Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who opposed Gandhi's advocacy of nonviolence and his friendship with Indian Muslims, shot him three times in the chest in the garden of Birla House in Delhi on his way to a prayer meeting. Gandhi's birthday, 2 October, is a national holiday in India, Gandhi Jayanti, and is marked worldwide as the International Day of Nonviolence. He is regarded as the Father of the Nation in India and was often called Bapu. His pamphlet Hind Swaraj of 1909 became the intellectual blueprint of the independence movement. Writers differ on him, some presenting a paragon of ethical living and others a more complex, contradictory and changing figure.
mainz: Mainz lies on the left bank of the Rhine at the northern end of the Upper Rhine Plain, opposite the mouth of the Main. Its name does not come from the river but is a simplification of Mogontiacum, a name that appears to be Celtic, probably linked to the Gallic god Mogons whom Roman soldiers had adopted. The city is in one of Germany's important wine regions.

The Roman general Nero Claudius Drusus founded the stronghold of Mogontiacum, perhaps as early as 13 or 12 BCE, on the northern frontier of the empire, and it became the capital of the province of Germania Superior. The Emperor Julian liberated the city in 357, and in 451 Attila's Huns sacked it. The Franks settled there from 459.

In the early Middle Ages Mainz played a significant part in the Christianisation of the German and Slavic peoples. Its first archbishop, Boniface, was killed in 754 while trying to convert the Frisians. The archbishopric was established in 781, when Boniface's successor Lullus received the pallium from Pope Adrian I, and the archbishops held high office in the Holy Roman Empire as archchancellors. A Jewish community existed from the 10th century and was known for its teaching, notably that of Rabbi Gershom ben Judah (960–1040). From the 12th century Mainz belonged to the ShUM cities with Speyer and Worms.

French revolutionary troops occupied the city in 1792, and on 18 March 1793 the Jacobins of Mainz proclaimed a Republic of Mainz under Georg Forster. After an 18-week siege the French surrendered to the Prussians on 23 July 1793. In 1816 Mainz became the capital of Rhenish Hesse, and until 1866 it was the chief fortress of the German Confederation against France.

Mainz is the capital and largest city of Rhineland-Palatinate, with about 223,000 inhabitants. It is the birthplace of Johannes Gutenberg, and its cathedral, one of the three Rhenish Imperial Cathedrals, is over a thousand years old. Roman remains include Jupiter's column, and the ShUM sites of Speyer, Worms and Mainz are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
maize: Maize, Zea mays, is a tall annual grass with a single stem, ranging in height from 1.2 to 4 m. The tassel at the top bears the male flowers, and a female inflorescence lower down develops into an ear wrapped in husks. The grains are usually yellow or white in modern varieties but can be orange, red, brown, blue, purple or black. Maize relies on humans for its propagation, since its kernels, unlike those of its wild ancestor teosinte, do not fall off the cob on their own.

The teosinte origin theory was proposed by the botanist Nikolai Vavilov in 1931 and by George Beadle in 1932. In 2004 John Doebley identified Balsas teosinte, native to the Balsas River valley in Mexico's south-western highlands, as the wild relative most similar to maize. All maize arose from a single domestication in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. Stone milling tools with maize residue have been found in an 8,700-year-old layer in a cave near Iguala, Guerrero, and maize reached highland Ecuador at least 8,000 years ago.
The Olmec and Maya cultivated it in numerous varieties and processed it by nixtamalization, and by 3,000 years ago it was central to Olmec culture, including their calendar, language and myths.

The niacin in maize is not available without nixtamalization, the alkali treatment, and the Maya made nixtamal meal into porridges and tamales. After 1492 explorers and traders carried maize to Europe. Spanish settlers preferred wheat bread, and maize flour could not replace wheat in communion bread, since only wheat was believed able to undergo transubstantiation. Maize was nevertheless grown in Spain within a few decades of Columbus's voyages, and by the 18th century it was the chief food of the southern French and Italian peasantry, especially as polenta.
majeerteen: The Majeerteen, also known as Mohammed Harti, belong to the Harti branch of the Darod. They traditionally inhabit the Bari, Nugaal and Mudug regions, from Bosaso to Garacad, between the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, and are most numerous in the regional capitals of Bosaso, Garowe and Galkacyo. Migrations that began in the 19th century took some to Kismayo in the south, and some live in the Dollo Zone of the Somali Region of Ethiopia. Historically the clan formed part of a coastal trading network around the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.

The first recorded mention of the clan in English is by Henry Salt, who described them as living on the coast of Hafun under a Sultan Hassan. Salt relates that the Imam of Muscat had sent gifts and asked leave to build a small fort there, and that both the request and the gifts were refused. In the 19th century Majeerteen merchants were active across the Red Sea. One of them, Ahmed Muhammad, was granted the island of Baka by the Damoheita Afar, and his family ruled it as sultans into the period of Italian rule in Eritrea.

The Majeerteen Sultanate was founded in the 15th or 16th century and rose to prominence in the 19th under Boqor Osman Mahamuud. It was nearly destroyed by his struggle with his cousin Yusuf Ali Kenadid, who was forced into exile in Yemen, returned with a band of Hadhrami musketeers, overpowered the local Hawiye clans and founded the Sultanate of Hobyo in 1878.

Kenadid signed a protectorate treaty with Italy, and Boqor Osman followed in late 1889. Each hoped to use Italian support against the other and to avoid direct occupation. When Kenadid refused to let British troops land in his territory to fight the Dervish forces of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, the Italians exiled him to Aden and then to Eritrea. After two years of resistance by Boqor Osman and Majeerteen rebels, which Italian forces put down with long coastal bombardments of towns and naval blockades, the territory came under the full authority of Rome by late 1927.

Osman Yusuf Kenadid, a son of the first sultan of Hobyo, devised the Osmanya script for the Somali language in the 1920s. Members of the clan held many government posts in the 1960s and 1970s, among them Abdirashid Shermarke, the first prime minister and second president of Somalia. In the 1980s and 1990s the Somali Salvation Democratic Front was a predominantly Majeerteen political group.
malawi: Malawi is a landlocked country in Southeast Africa, bordered by Zambia, Tanzania and Mozambique. The Great Rift Valley runs through it from north to south, and Lake Malawi, also called Lake Nyasa, makes up over three-quarters of its eastern boundary. The lake is about 587 kilometres long and 84 kilometres wide, and the Shire River flows from its southern end to join the Zambezi in Mozambique. South of the lake lie the Shire Highlands, where the Zomba and Mulanje peaks rise. The altitude moderates what would otherwise be an equatorial climate, with rains between November and April.

The name Malawi means 'flames' in Chichewa and Chitumbuka and was chosen by the first president, Hastings Banda, after independence in 1964. It comes from the Maravi, a Bantu ethnic group that emigrated from the southern Congo around 1400.

Before the arrival of Bantu peoples from the north around the 10th century CE, the area had a small population of hunter-gatherers, known in oral tradition as Akafula or BaTwa, who were gradually overtaken by agrarian Bantu peoples. By the 16th century the Bantu groups had established kingdoms such as the Maravi Empire, which reached from north of Nkhotakota to the Zambezi River, and the Nkhamanga. In the 17th century, with the area mostly united under one ruler, people began trading and making alliances with Portuguese traders and soldiers. By the 18th century the empire had broken up.

The Indian Ocean slave trade reached its height in the mid-19th century, when about 20,000 people a year are believed to have been enslaved and taken from Nkhotakota to Kilwa. David Livingstone reached Lake Malawi in 1859 and identified the Shire Highlands as suitable for European settlement.

Anglican and Presbyterian missions followed Livingstone's visit in the 1860s and 1870s, the African Lakes Company was established in 1878, and a British consul took up residence at Blantyre in 1883. To prevent Portuguese occupation, the British government sent Harry Johnston as consul to make treaties with local rulers. In 1891 the area became the British Central African Protectorate, renamed Nyasaland in 1907. Nyasaland became independent under Hastings Banda in 1964.

Malawi is the Republic of Malawi, with its capital and largest city at Lilongwe and its commercial centre at Blantyre. English is the official language, and Chichewa, Chitumbuka and Chiyao are major regional languages. Lake Malawi National Park, listed in 1984, and the Chongoni Rock Art Area, listed in 2006, are its two UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
malay-language: Historical linguists agree that the Malayic homeland was probably in western Borneo. A form called Proto-Malayic was spoken there by at least 1000 BCE and is argued to be the ancestor of all later Malayic languages. Its own ancestor, Proto-Malayo-Polynesian, began to break up by at least 2000 BCE, possibly through the southward expansion of Austronesian peoples from Taiwan.

Old Malay, believed to be the ancestor of Classical Malay, was influenced by Sanskrit. The earliest known stone inscription in Old Malay, the Kedukan Bukit inscription, was found on Sumatra near Palembang and is dated 1 May 683, written in the Pallava variety of the Grantha alphabet. Srivijaya, a maritime empire based on Sumatra from the 7th to the 11th centuries, spread Old Malay through the Malay Peninsula and Archipelago, where it served as the lingua franca of traders in ports and marketplaces.

The Terengganu Inscription Stone, dated approximately to 1303 CE and written in Jawi script, is considered the earliest evidence of Classical Malay. Its ruler urges his subjects to uphold Islam and sets out ten basic laws. Classical Malay came into wide use as a lingua franca under the Malacca Sultanate (1402 to 1511), a hub of trade and Islamic learning. Islamic literature brought a large infusion of Arabic vocabulary, alongside continued influence from Sanskrit and Tamil.

After the Portuguese captured Malacca in 1511 the court re-established itself as the Johor Sultanate and kept Classical Malay as its literary and administrative language, while literary centres dispersed to Aceh, Java, Makassar, the Moluccas and Champa. In the 19th century the Dutch and British, divided by the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824, both used Malay as a tool of centralisation and modernisation.

Before Arabic script arrived, Malay was written in the Pallava, Kawi and Rencong scripts. From the era of the Kingdom of Pasai and the golden age of Malacca, Jawi gradually replaced them. From the 17th century, under Dutch and British influence, the Latin script Rumi gradually replaced Jawi.

Malay is an Austronesian pluricentric macrolanguage, native to several islands of Maritime Southeast Asia and the Malay Peninsula. It is an official language of Brunei, Malaysia and Singapore, where its standard form is Standard Malay, and Indonesian, an autonomous standard, is the official language of Indonesia. It is spoken as a first language by about 80 million people and as a first or second language by close to 300 million. Latin script is official in Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, and Jawi is co-official with it in Brunei and Malaysia.
malayalam-language: The origin of Malayalam is disputed. The mainstream view holds that it descends from a western coastal dialect of early Middle Tamil, which began to separate in the 8th century and became distinct between the 9th and 13th centuries. The Western Ghats isolate the Malabar Coast, and Sanskrit and Prakrit influence from the Nambudiri Brahmins helped the dialect to diverge. A second view, generally rejected by historical linguists, holds that Tamil and Malayalam developed separately from a common ancestor. Some scholars treat the Quilon Syrian copper plates of 849 or 850 CE as the oldest inscription in Old Malayalam, though others regard the language of such inscriptions as a variety of Tamil. The Malayalam calendar dates from 825 CE.

Malayalam is the majority language of Kerala and an official language in Kerala, Lakshadweep and Mahé in Puducherry. At the census of 2011 there were 32,413,213 speakers in Kerala. Its word order is subject-object-verb, and verbs are conjugated for tense, mood and aspect but not for person, gender or number. It has borrowed most from Sanskrit and later English, and also from Arabic, Dutch, Persian, Portuguese and Syriac. Besides its own script it has been written in others: Suriyani Malayalam, in a Syriac script, was used by the Saint Thomas Christians until the 20th century, and Arabi Malayalam, in an Arabic script, until the early 20th century.

Folk songs, the oldest literary form, were oral. The Ramacharitam, of the late 12th or early 13th century, is the oldest extant work distinct from the Tamil tradition. Middle Malayalam was shaped by Manipravalam, a blend of Tamil and Sanskrit whose name means ruby-coral. Cherusseri Namboothiri's Krishnagatha, written for the court of Udaya Varman Kolathiri in the 15th century, appears to be the first work in the present-day language. In the 16th century Thunchaththu Ezhuthachan wrote the Adhyathmaramayanam Kilippattu. The first travelogue in any Indian language is the Malayalam Varthamanappusthakam, by Paremmakkal Thoma Kathanar in 1785. Later writers include Thakazhi Sivasankara Pillai, M. T. Vasudevan Nair, Vaikom Muhammed Basheer and Arundhati Roy.
malcolm-x: Malcolm X was born on 19 May 1925 in Omaha, Nebraska, the fourth of seven children of Louise Little, born in Grenada, and the Reverend Earl Little, a Baptist minister. Both parents admired the Pan-African activist Marcus Garvey and led the local branch of his Universal Negro Improvement Association, and they taught their children self-reliance and black pride. In 1946 he was sentenced to eight to ten years in prison for larceny and burglary. There he met a fellow convict, John Bembry, who gave him a voracious appetite for reading, and joined the Nation of Islam, taking the name Malcolm X in place of what he called the white slavemaster name of Little.

After his parole in August 1952 Malcolm X rose quickly in the Nation. He took charge of Temple Number 7 in Harlem in 1954 and became its public face for twelve years, preaching black empowerment and the separation of Black and white Americans, and criticising Martin Luther King Jr. and the mainstream civil rights movement for its emphasis on non-violence and integration. The Federal Bureau of Investigation began watching him in 1953. He is credited with helping the Nation grow from about 1,200 members in the early 1950s to an estimated 50,000 to 100,000 by the early 1960s.

On 8 March 1964 he announced that he was leaving the Nation. He founded Muslim Mosque, Inc., a religious organisation, and the Organization of Afro-American Unity, a secular group advocating Pan-Africanism. In April 1964 he made the Hajj to Mecca, and he then toured Africa.

Throughout 1964 Malcolm X received death threats as his conflict with the Nation intensified. On 21 February 1965 he was shot as he prepared to address the Organization of Afro-American Unity at the Audubon Ballroom in Manhattan. Three Nation of Islam members were convicted, and in 2021 two of the convictions were vacated. Whether others conceived or aided the killing has been debated since.

Apart from his autobiography, written with Alex Haley and published posthumously in 1965, Malcolm X left no published writings, and his philosophy is known from his speeches and interviews. His ideas were an important influence on the Black power movement.
mali: Mali is a landlocked country of 1,240,192 square kilometres in West Africa, the eighth largest in Africa. Its northern borders reach deep into the Sahara Desert, and most of the country lies in the southern Sahara, while southern Mali, where the majority of inhabitants live, is in the Sudanian savanna. The Niger and Senegal rivers run through the south. Late April to early October is the rainy season there, and flooding of the Niger is common, creating the Inner Niger Delta. The Adrar des Ifoghas massif lies in the northeast, and gold, uranium, phosphates, salt and limestone are among its natural resources.

Rock art in the Sahara suggests that northern Mali has been inhabited since about 10,000 BCE, when the Sahara was fertile. Early ceramics from Ounjougou, dating to about 9,400 BCE, are believed to show an independent invention of pottery. Farming took place by 5000 BCE and iron was used by around 500 BCE. In the first millennium BCE Mandé peoples related to the Soninke created early towns along the middle Niger, among them Dia, from around 900 BCE, and Djenné-Djenno, which lasted from around 300 BCE to 900 CE.

Mali was part of three successive West African empires that controlled this trade: the Ghana Empire, the Mali Empire and the Songhai Empire. At its peak in 1300 the Mali Empire was the wealthiest country in Africa, and Mansa Musa is believed to have been one of the wealthiest individuals in history. Medieval Mali was a centre of Islam, culture and knowledge, and Timbuktu became a notable place of education.

The Songhai Empire absorbed the Mali Empire in 1468, and a Saadian army defeated the Songhai in 1591. In the late 19th century France seized control during the Scramble for Africa and made it part of French Sudan. It became independent in 1960, first in a brief federation with Senegal, and then as the Republic of Mali.

Bamako is the capital and largest city. The name Mali comes from the Mali Empire and originally meant hippopotamus, the clan symbol of the Keita dynasty. Most people live in the south, and the Bambara are the largest ethnic group, with the Fulani, Senufo, Malinke, Soninke, Dogon, Songhai and Tuareg among others. Malian musical tradition derives from the griots, the Keepers of Memories, and literary tradition is passed mainly by word of mouth, with jalis reciting histories and stories known by heart.
malta: Malta is an archipelago in the central Mediterranean, about 80 kilometres from southern Italy across the Malta Channel. Only Malta, Gozo and Comino have permanent residents, and Comino is practically uninhabited. The islands lie on a shallow shelf that was once part of a land bridge between Sicily and North Africa, and the archipelago sits on the African tectonic plate. The terrain is coarse and hilly, with many harbours along an indented coastline. The highest point, Ta' Dmejrek near Dingli, is 253 metres high, and Malta has no rivers or lakes.

The earliest reliable evidence of habitation dates to 6500 BCE, when Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, probably from Sicily, arrived. Neolithic farmers from Sicily are thought to have followed by around 5400 BCE. Around 3500 BCE the islanders built the Ġgantija temples on Gozo, among the oldest free-standing structures in the world, and other early temples include those at Ħaġar Qim and Mnajdra. After 2500 BCE Malta was depopulated until a new people arrived who cremated their dead and built small dolmens as tombs; they probably differed from the temple builders.

Phoenician traders colonised the islands around 1000 BCE, with their seat of government at Mdina and their main port at Cospicua on the Grand Harbour, which they called Maleth. Carthage controlled the islands after the fall of Phoenicia. It is unsure whether Roman rule began after the first or second Punic War, but Rome held Malta after the second, when it was surrendered by Hamilcar, a son of Gisco, to the consul Titus Sempronius Longus. The Arabs, Normans and Aragonese ruled in the Middle Ages, and the Knights Hospitaller, French and British in the modern era.

Malta became a British crown colony in the early 19th century and served as headquarters of the British Mediterranean Fleet. It was besieged by the Axis powers in the Second World War. Independence came in 1964, and the current parliamentary republic was established in 1974. Malta joined the European Union in 2004 and the eurozone on 1 January 2008.

The two official languages are Maltese, a Semitic language with close ties to Arabic and Sicilian, and English. Catholicism is the state religion, though the constitution guarantees freedom of religion. The 2025 census counted 588,254 people.
maltese-language: Maltese is a Central Semitic language derived from late medieval Sicilian Arabic. The pioneering Maltese linguists Giovanni Pietro Francesco Agius de Soldanis and Mikiel Anton Vassalli both hypothesised that it came from the Punic language, a view that later scholars did not accept. The language is generally traced to the arrival, early in the 11th century, of settlers from neighbouring Sicily, where Siculo-Arabic was spoken.

The Norman conquest of 1091, followed by the expulsion of the Muslims, complete by 1249, permanently isolated the vernacular from its Arabic source and created the conditions for its evolution into a distinct language. In Sicily, Siculo-Arabic became extinct and was replaced by Sicilian, but in Malta the vernacular continued to develop alongside Italian. The first written reference to it is in a will of 1436, where it is called lingua maltensi, and the oldest known document in Maltese is the 15th-century poem Il-Kantilena by Pietru Caxaro.

Maltese is spoken by the Maltese people and is a national language of Malta. It is the only standardised Semitic language written exclusively in the Latin script. The core vocabulary, including the most common words and the function words, is Semitic, and the Arabic base makes up around one third of the vocabulary. About half of the vocabulary comes from standard Italian and Sicilian, and English words make up between 6 and 20 per cent. The rural dialects keep archaic features and use more Semitic roots and broken plurals than Standard Maltese. The modern spelling system was introduced in 1924.

Under the Knights Hospitaller both French and Italian were used for official documents, and in the British colonial period English was encouraged through education, with Italian as the next most important language. Hieronymus Megiser, who visited Malta in 1588 and 1589, included a list of Maltese words in two works, and Agius de Soldanis produced the first systematic lexicon and grammar and proposed a standard orthography. Late in the 18th century and through the 19th, Vassalli and others made a concerted effort to standardise the written language. Maltese was recognised as an official language, alongside English, in 1934. Its use declined under British administration relative to English, and after independence language reforms increased its use.
managua: Managua stands on the southern shore of Lake Managua, also called Lake Xolotlán, in western Nicaragua, with a tropical wet and dry climate and two seasons: a rainy season from mid-May to mid-November and a dry one for the rest of the year. The lake has been polluted by the dumping of chemicals and waste water since 1927, and a waste-water treatment plant at Las Mercedes, funded by the German government, was inaugurated in 2009. The name may come from the Nahuatl mana-ahuac, 'adjacent to the water', or from a word in the Mangue language meaning 'place of the big man' or 'chief'.

The area was inhabited by Paleo-Indians as far back as 12,000 BCE. The footprints of Acahualinca, fossilised in volcanic ash along the shore, are 2,100 years old. Founded as a pre-Columbian fishing town, the settlement was incorporated in 1819 as Leal Villa de Santiago de Managua. Efforts to make it the capital began in 1824, after the Central American nations attained independence from Spain, and Nicaragua became an independent nation in 1838. Its position between the rival cities of León and Granada made it a logical compromise, and it was officially selected as the national capital in 1852. Between 1842 and 1930 it expanded and urbanised rapidly.

A disastrous earthquake in 1931 destroyed much of the city and killed between 1,000 and 2,450 people, and a large fire in 1936 destroyed much of what was left. Under the rule of Anastasio Somoza García and his family, from 1936 to 1979, the city was rebuilt and grew rapidly, with new government buildings, industry and universities. The earthquake of 1972 destroyed 90 percent of the city. Among the few buildings to survive were the National Palace, the Rubén Darío National Theatre and, though heavily damaged, the Old Cathedral, built from 1928 to 1938 as the first cathedral in the Western Hemisphere made entirely of concrete on a metal frame. The New Cathedral, designed by Ricardo Legorreta, was inaugurated in 1993 to replace it.

Managua is the capital and largest city of Nicaragua, with an estimated population of 1,063,815 in 2023, and the main economic, political and cultural hub of the country. Most of its universities are there, among them the National Autonomous University of Nicaragua, established in 1812 at León. The Plaza de la Revolución, on the shore of the lake, holds its historic centre, the Old Cathedral, the National Palace of Culture, which houses the National Museum, and the Rubén Darío National Theatre. The Museum of Acahualinca preserves the ancient footprints. The city's patron saint, Santo Domingo de Guzmán, is honoured each August in a festival in which his statue is carried across the city.
manama: Manama lies in the north-eastern corner of Bahrain on a small peninsula along the Persian Gulf. The land is flat and arid, with extremely hot summers and mild winters, and reclaimed land has extended the coastline in recent decades. Its coastal position made it a port and trading point of the Gulf. Historically the city was confined to what is now the Manama Souq and the Manama Fort to its south, and it has since grown to take in suburban developments and older neighbouring villages.

There is evidence of human settlement on Bahrain's northern coastline from the Bronze Age. The Dilmun civilisation inhabited the area in 3000 BCE as a trading hub between Mesopotamia, Magan and the Indus Valley Civilisation, and about 100,000 Dilmun burial mounds have been found across the north and centre of the country. The name Manamah is first recorded around 730 AH, about 1330 CE, during a visit by Turan Shah of Hurmuz to the island. Manama remained a small trading port until the Portuguese took control in the early 1500s, and in 1602 the Safavid Persians expelled them. The Safavids sidelined Manama and made the nearby town of Bilad Al Qadeem the provincial capital, while the islands' pearl exports grew.

The twin towns of Manama and Muharraq appear to have been founded together in the 1800s. Muharraq, with its more defensible position, was the capital of Bahrain until 1923, while Manama became the mercantile capital and the gateway to the main island. After the outbreak of the First World War in 1914 the British Raj used Manama as a base for the Mesopotamian campaign, and a municipal government was established there in 1919. In the 1920s the British pressed administrative reforms, including a reorganised customs office in 1923, civil courts, and in 1926 the appointment of Charles Belgrave as financial adviser. Manama was declared the capital when Bahrain became independent in 1971.

Manama is the capital and largest city of Bahrain, and its population has long been cosmopolitan: in 1904 it was estimated at 25,000, half of them foreigners from Basra, Najd, al-Hasa, Iran, India and Europe. Shia and Sunni Islam have coexisted there for centuries, each represented by distinct ethnic groups. Oil wealth spurred growth in the 20th century, and diversification from the 1990s made the city a financial hub of the Persian Gulf and a centre of Islamic banking. Bab Al Bahrain and the adjacent souq are among its notable cultural sites, and the city centre is the main location of Muharram processions in the country.
manas-river: The Manas, known in Bhutan as the Drangme Chhu, is the largest of Bhutan's four major river systems. It drains 41,350 square kilometres of eastern Bhutan and northeast India through three main branches, the Drangme Chhu, the Mangde Chhu and the Bumthang or Chamkhar Chhu. Part of its main stem rises in southern Tibet at about 4,500 metres and enters India in the Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh before crossing into Bhutan near Trashigang. The Lhobrak or Kuri Chhu, its main central tributary, is the only one that rises north of the Great Himalayas.

In Bhutan the river runs southwest through V-shaped gorges between two ranges of the Lower Himalayas. In the foothills the valley widens into swamps and marshes. The Aie River joins it in Assam, and it then meanders for about 75 kilometres to the Brahmaputra near Jogighopa. It is the largest tributary on the Brahmaputra's north bank and contributes 5.48 per cent of its average volume. From May to October the southwest monsoon brings more than 4,000 millimetres of rain to the southern part of the basin; the flow in the monsoon is said to be as much as 20 times that of the dry season.

The core of the present Manas Wildlife Sanctuary in Assam was designated a sanctuary in 1928 and declared a tiger reserve in 1978; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in December 1985. A dam proposed in the 1970s would have sent a canal 100 kilometres long through the tiger reserve to the Sankosh River. India's Ministry of Environment and Forests objected, the World Heritage Committee of UNESCO supported the objection, and Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi discontinued the project. Two dams proposed on the Bhutanese side were dropped in 1986. In February 1989 members of the All Bodo Students Union entered the park and killed several wardens and guards.

The lowlands north of the confluence, the Duars, are very fertile and have been made into tea estates and paddy fields. Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan, raised to a national park in 1993, is 92 per cent forested, and five thousand people live in villages inside it. The two reserves shelter the Bengal tiger, Asian elephant, greater one-horned rhinoceros, wild water buffalo, pygmy hog, hispid hare and golden langur, and the Ganges river dolphin lives in the river.
mandarin-chinese: The hundreds of modern local varieties of Chinese developed from regional variants of Old Chinese and Middle Chinese. Besides Mandarin, six other major groups are traditionally recognised: Wu, Gan, Xiang, Min, Hakka and Yue. Mandarin originated in North China, and its spread is attributed to the greater ease of travel on the North China Plain compared with the mountainous south.

After the fall of the Northern Song in 1126, and under the Jin and the Yuan dynasties in northern China, a common form of speech developed from the dialects of the North China Plain around the capital, called Old Mandarin. New genres of vernacular literature were written in it. The Zhongyuan Yinyun, a rime dictionary of 1324, records many features of modern Mandarin, such as the disappearance of final plosives.

Mandarin is the largest branch of the Sinitic languages. Mandarin varieties are natively spoken by 71 per cent of all Chinese speakers, over an area stretching from Yunnan in the southwest to Xinjiang in the northwest and Heilongjiang in the northeast. Many varieties are not mutually intelligible with the Beijing dialect. Most have four lexical tones, and many keep retroflex initial consonants, which southern varieties have lost. Chinese languages are strongly analytic, relying on word order and particles rather than inflection.

The English word mandarin originally meant an official of the Ming and Qing empires. These officials, whose native varieties were often mutually unintelligible, ran the empire in a koiné based on northern varieties called Guānhuà, the language of the officials; Jesuit missionaries who learned it in the 16th century called it Mandarin. Until the early 20th century formal writing was in Literary Chinese, but a literature in written vernacular Chinese had grown up from at least the Yuan dynasty, with Water Margin and Dream of the Red Chamber.

After the Republic's founding, intellectuals of the New Culture Movement, among them Hu Shih and Chen Duxiu, campaigned to replace Literary Chinese with it. The National Language Unification Commission settled on the Beijing dialect as the national standard in 1932, and the People's Republic, founded in 1949, kept it as pǔtōnghuà. Singapore's Speak Mandarin Campaign began in 1979.
manghud: The Manghud belonged to the Urud-Manghud federation of the Mongolian plateau, and ancient sources derive them from the Kiyat Mongols. The Persian historian Rashid-al-Din Hamadani, who chronicled the Mongols, claimed that many old Mongol clans, the Manghud among them, were founded by members of the Borjigin.

Some Manghud warriors supported Genghis Khan, while a body of them resisted his rise to power. As the Mongol Empire expanded, the Manghud were carried westward with many other Mongol tribes. The clan name was also used for Mongol vanguard troops, though sources differ widely on the military units called mangudai.

In the Golden Horde the Manghud supported Nogai, who died in 1299, and formed a horde of their own, semi-independent of the khans at Sarai. After Nogai's death most of their warriors entered the service of Tokhta Khan. Edigu, who lived from 1352 to 1419 and was the son of the noble Kutlukiya, led the eastern begs and by the end of the 14th century dominated the Golden Horde.

The Nogais guarded the northern borders of the Astrakhan and Crimean khanates and by organised raids into the northern steppes prevented Russian and Lithuanian settlement. Many entered the service of the Crimean khan and contributed to the formation of the Crimean Tatars. About 1630 the Kalmyks, migrating from southern Siberia to the lower Volga, drove the Nogais out; they fled to the plains of the northern Caucasus and to the Crimea, and a small part joined the Kazakh Khanate.

Other Manghits had been settled by Genghis Khan around the city of Qarshi, which remained their base under the Khanate of Bukhara. Their power there grew in the early 18th century through the office of ataliq to the khan. After the death of Nader Shah in 1747 the ataliq Muhammad Rahim Bi had the ruling Abu al-Fayz Khan and his young son killed. The family ruled behind the scenes until the 1780s, when the emir Shah Murad declared himself ruler openly. Not being descendants of Genghis Khan, the Manghits took the Islamic title of emir, not khan, and based their legitimacy on Islam.

The last emir, Mohammed Alim Khan, was ousted by the Soviet Red Army in September 1920 and fled to Afghanistan. Whether his dynasty was of Mongol or of plain Uzbek origin is disputed. The Nogai and Karakalpak peoples are counted among the descendants of the Manghud, and Manghits are found among the Tatars of Russia, the Bashkirs and the Kazakhs, as well as among the Khalkha Mongols of Mongolia.
manhattan: Manhattan is the geographically smallest of the five boroughs of New York City and is coextensive with New York County. It lies almost entirely on Manhattan Island, bounded by the Hudson River to the west and the East River to the east, while the Harlem River divides it from the Bronx. The island is 13.4 miles long and 2.3 miles wide at its widest point, near 14th Street, and is loosely divided into Lower Manhattan, Midtown and Upper Manhattan. Its bedrock of Inwood marble, Fordham gneiss and Manhattan schist is well suited to the foundations of skyscrapers.

Manhattan was part of Lenapehoking, the territory of the Munsee, Lenape and Wappinger peoples. Their main trail, from what is now Inwood to Battery Park, later became Broadway. Giovanni da Verrazzano, sailing for Francis I of France, became the first documented European to visit the area, in April 1524. Dutch colonists set up a trading post on the island in 1624, named New Amsterdam in 1626. The English took the territory in 1664 and renamed it New York for the Duke of York.

Manhattan was at the heart of the New York Campaign in the American Revolutionary War, and the Continental Army abandoned it after the Battle of Fort Washington on 16 November 1776. British occupation lasted until 25 November 1783. New York was the capital of the United States from 1785 until 1790, and by 1810 it was the most populous city in the country. The Commissioners' Plan of 1811 laid out the grid, and the Erie Canal opened in 1825. The subway opened in 1904, and Manhattan became a borough in the consolidation of 1898.

Manhattan had 1,694,250 residents at the 2020 census, in a land area of about 22.7 square miles. It is the economic and administrative centre of New York City, with City Hall, Wall Street, the New York Stock Exchange and the headquarters of the United Nations in Turtle Bay. Central Park, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux in the 1850s, covers 840 acres. The Statue of Liberty is part of the borough, and its landmarks include the Empire State Building, Grand Central Terminal and Times Square.
manila: Manila lies on the eastern shore of Manila Bay, on the western coast of the island of Luzon, 1,300 kilometres from mainland Asia. The protected harbour is regarded as the finest in Asia. The Pasig River flows through the middle of the city and divides it into northern and southern sections. Almost all of the city sits on prehistoric alluvial deposits built by the Pasig and on land reclaimed from the bay. The name derives from Maynilà, commonly interpreted as the place where indigo plants are abundant, from the Sanskrit nīla; it was probably given for the plants growing around the settlement, since indigo extraction became important in the area only in the 18th century.

The earliest evidence of human life near Manila is the Angono Petroglyphs, dated to around 3000 BCE. By 1258 a fortified Tagalog polity called Maynila existed on the site, and with Tondo it traded with the Song and Yuan dynasties of China. In 1365 both Brunei and Manila were conquered by the Majapahit Empire, which named Manila Selurong in Sanskrit texts.

On 24 June 1571, after Rajah Sulayman, the polity's last indigenous ruler, was defeated at the Battle of Bangkusay, the Spanish conquistador Miguel López de Legazpi began building the walled fortification of Intramuros. Manila became the capital of the captaincy general of the Spanish East Indies, administered for the Spanish crown from Mexico City in the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Its commercial networks were the first to extend across the Pacific Ocean and connect Asia with the Spanish Americas through the galleon trade.

Under American occupation Manila became the first chartered city in the country, by Philippine Commission Act No. 183 of 31 July 1901, and in 1905 Daniel Burnham was commissioned to design the new capital on the principles of the City Beautiful movement. During the Second World War it was razed by Japanese forces and by American shelling. It became autonomous with the Revised Charter of 18 June 1949, and most historical buildings were reconstructed, though many in Intramuros were damaged beyond repair.

Manila is the capital of the Philippines and its second most populous city after Quezon City, with 1,902,590 people in the 2024 census. It has 16 administrative districts, and the name is also used for Metro Manila, the capital region. The National Museum Complex in Rizal Park holds Juan Luna's painting Spoliarium, and the historic Walled City of Intramuros is administered by a national agency, the Intramuros Administration.
manitoba: Manitoba lies at the longitudinal centre of Canada, bordered by Nunavut and the Northwest Territories to the north, Hudson Bay to the northeast, Ontario to the east, North Dakota and Minnesota to the south and Saskatchewan to the west. Its landscape runs from arctic tundra and the Hudson Bay coast in the north to boreal forest, large freshwater lakes and prairie in the centre and south. It lies at the centre of the Hudson Bay drainage basin, where much of the water drains into Lake Winnipeg and then north down the Nelson River. Most of the inhabited south developed in the bed of the prehistoric Glacial Lake Agassiz, and the Red River Valley is flat and fertile.

First Nations peoples settled the area about 10,000 years ago, shortly after the last ice age glaciers retreated. The Ojibwe, Cree, Dene, Sioux, Mandan and Assiniboine founded settlements, and the first farming was along the Red River, where corn and other seed crops were planted before contact with Europeans. English and French fur traders arrived in the early 17th century. England secured the region in 1670 as Rupert's Land under the Hudson's Bay Company, and the early economy centred on the trade of beaver pelts and other furs. Lord Selkirk brought the first agricultural settlers in 1811, and a Red River Colony of Indigenous and Métis people grew up.

Deep disagreements over self-determination during the transfer of Rupert's Land to Canada in 1869 led to armed resistance under the Métis leader Louis Riel, who established a provisional government. Its assembly sent three delegates to Ottawa, and the negotiations produced the Manitoba Act, introduced by Prime Minister Sir John A. Macdonald, which made Manitoba the fifth province of Canada in 1870. The name was chosen by Thomas Spence, and Riel preferred it to the alternative Assiniboia. Riel fled into exile, and the Canadian government blocked the Métis' attempts to obtain the land promised to them. Facing racism from a flood of settlers from Ontario, many Métis moved to what became Saskatchewan and Alberta.

By 1911 Winnipeg was the third largest city in Canada. Nellie McClung led the campaign for women's votes, and on 28 January 1916 Manitoba became the first province to allow women to vote in provincial elections, two years before Canada did so nationally.

Manitoba is a province of Canada with Winnipeg as its capital and largest city, home to nearly two thirds of the provincial population in its metropolitan region. English and French are both official languages of its legislature and courts under the Manitoba Act, a status the Supreme Court of Canada upheld in 1985. The population was 1,342,153 at the 2021 census. The Winnipeg-based Royal Winnipeg Ballet, granted its royal title in 1953, is Canada's oldest ballet company.
mao-zedong: Mao Zedong was born on 26 December 1893 near Shaoshan village in Hunan, under the Qing dynasty. His father, Mao Yichang, was a formerly impoverished peasant who had become one of the wealthiest farmers in Shaoshan. He preferred classic novels such as Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Water Margin to the Confucian texts he was taught. At 13 he was married by arrangement to Luo Yixiu, whom he refused to recognise as his wife.

In Beijing he worked as assistant to the Peking University librarian Li Dazhao, an early Chinese Communist, whose articles on the October Revolution added Marxism to the doctrines of the Chinese revolutionary movement. Mao joined Li's Study Group and developed rapidly toward Marxism in the winter of 1919. In 1921 he became a founding member of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).

After Chiang Kai-shek turned on the Communists in 1927, the CCP lost about 15,000 of its 25,000 members. The party founded the Workers' and Peasants' Red Army, and Mao was made its commander-in-chief. His Autumn Harvest Uprising against Changsha failed, and on 15 September he marched east with 1,000 survivors to the Jinggang Mountains of Jiangxi. In 1935 he became leader of the CCP during the Long March, a retreat to the Yan'an Soviet in Shaanxi. The civil war resumed after Japan's surrender in 1945, and the Nationalist government withdrew to Taiwan in 1949.

Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China from Tiananmen on 1 October 1949. He sent the People's Volunteer Army into the Korean War in October 1950. From 1958 to 1962 he oversaw the Great Leap Forward, which aimed to collectivise agriculture and industrialise the country and was followed by the Great Chinese Famine. In 1966 he launched the Cultural Revolution, marked by violent class struggle, destruction of historical artifacts and a cult of personality.

Mao died shortly after midnight on 9 September 1976, aged 82, after three heart attacks that year. Despite his request to be cremated, his embalmed body was later placed on permanent display in a mausoleum. Historians and others judge his rule in different ways. His policies are held to have caused the deaths of tens of millions of people, mainly through starvation, but also through persecution, prison labour and executions. He is also credited with ending decades of civil war, improving literacy, education and the status of women. On 27 June 1981 the CCP Central Committee adopted a resolution stating that his contributions to the revolution far outweighed his mistakes.
maputo: Maputo stands on the west side of Maputo Bay, an inlet of the Indian Ocean 95 kilometres long and 30 kilometres wide, where the rivers Tembe, Umbeluzi, Matola and Infulene drain into the Espírito Santo Estuary. The island of Inhaca lies at the eastern end of the bay. The city is 120 kilometres from the South African border at Ressano Garcia and 80 kilometres from the border with Eswatini. Its economy has long centred on its port, through which much of the country's imports and exports pass.

The area was first settled as a fishing village by ancestors of the Tsonga people. It was named after the Portuguese navigator Lourenço Marques, who with António Caldeira was sent by the governor of Mozambique to explore the rivers flowing into Delagoa Bay in the mid-16th century. The forts and trading stations that the Portuguese established, abandoned and reoccupied on the north bank were all called Lourenço Marques. The existing town dates from about 1850, the earlier settlement having been entirely destroyed by the local people, and it grew around a Portuguese fortress. It was raised to city status in 1877.

In 1898 the colony of Portuguese Mozambique moved its capital there, and in the late 19th and early 20th centuries the city grew as a port. The main port handled 17 million tons of cargo in 1971, at its peak. Some of its best-known buildings date from this time, including the Central Train Station, built between 1913 and 1916 and sometimes mistaken for the work of Gustav Eiffel, and the Hotel Polana, designed by Herbert Baker.

The People's Republic of Mozambique was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 under the Lusaka Accord of September 1974. The capital had been expected to be renamed Can Phumo, after a Shangaan chief who lived there before the Portuguese arrived, but in February 1976 it became Maputo, a name tied to the Maputo River and to the FRELIMO slogan Hail Mozambique, united from the Rovuma to the Maputo. The civil war devastated its economy, and street names were changed to remove colonial figures and reflect ties with the Eastern Bloc.

Maputo is the capital and largest city of Mozambique, with 1,088,449 inhabitants in 2017 and 2,717,437 in the metropolitan area, which includes Matola. It is administered as a separate province. Its architecture mixes Portuguese colonial Neoclassical and Manueline styles with art deco and modernist buildings, and it is known as the City of Acacias. Eduardo Mondlane University, founded in 1968, is the oldest in the country.
marche: Marche is bordered by Emilia-Romagna and San Marino to the north, Tuscany and Umbria to the west, Lazio to the south-west, Abruzzo to the south and the Adriatic Sea to the east. It covers 9,366 square kilometres. Most of it is mountainous or hilly, and only Monte Vettore, at 2,476 metres, rises above 2,400 metres. The coastline is 173 kilometres long and mostly flat and straight. The name is the plural of the medieval word marca, a march or border zone, and first referred to border territories of the Holy Roman Empire such as the March of Ancona.

In ancient times the region was known as Picenum, and in the Iron Age it was almost entirely inhabited by the Picentes. In the fourth century BCE the Senones, a tribe of Gauls, occupied the north. After the Battle of Sentinum in 295 BCE the Romans founded numerous colonies there, linked to Rome by the Via Flaminia and the Via Salaria.
