After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the Goths invaded, and it was later part of the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna, with Ancona, Fano, Pesaro, Rimini and Senigallia forming the Pentapolis. Charlemagne conquered it in the late eighth century, and between the ninth and eleventh centuries the marches of Camerino, Fermo and Ancona were created.

Marche was nominally part of the Papal States, but most of it was held by local lords while the main cities ruled themselves as free communes. In the twelfth century the commune of Ancona resisted both Frederick Barbarossa and the Republic of Venice as a maritime republic. In the Renaissance rival families such as the Malatesta and the house of Montefeltro of Urbino fought over the region, and the Duchy of Urbino, the last independent entity, was dissolved in 1631. After Napoleon's defeat the region returned to papal rule until 4 November 1860, when a plebiscite annexed it to the unified Kingdom of Italy.

Marche is one of the twenty regions of Italy, with Ancona as its capital and largest city and a population of nearly 1.5 million. It is divided into five provinces: Ancona, Ascoli Piceno, Fermo, Macerata, and Pesaro and Urbino. Urbino, a major centre of Renaissance history, was the birthplace of Raphael, and the region is also the birthplace of Donato Bramante, Giacomo Leopardi, Gioachino Rossini and Maria Montessori. Castelfidardo is a centre for making accordions.
marco-polo: Marco Polo was born around 1254 in Venice, though the exact date and place of birth are not recorded in the archives. A few theories place his birth on the island of Korčula or in Constantinople, but most scholars have not accepted them. His father Niccolò Polo was a merchant who traded with the Near East. Niccolò and his brother Maffeo left on a trading voyage before Marco's birth and, according to The Travels of Marco Polo, passed through much of Asia and met Kublai Khan.

Marco's mother died, and an aunt and uncle raised him. He learned mercantile subjects such as foreign currency, appraising and the handling of cargo ships, and he learned little or no Latin. Around 1269 Niccolò returned to Venice and met his 15-year-old son for the first time.

Marco travelled through Asia along the Silk Road with his father and uncle until they reached Cathay and the court of Kublai Khan. Kublai was impressed by Marco's intelligence and humility and appointed him a foreign emissary, sent on diplomatic missions through the empire and Southeast Asia. He lived in the emperor's lands for 17 years. Around 1291 the Polos offered to accompany the Mongol princess Kököchin to Persia, where they arrived around 1293. They then went overland to Constantinople and Venice, returning home after many years away.

Venice was then at war with Genoa. Marco joined the war effort and was captured by the Genoese. In prison he dictated his stories to a cellmate, Rustichello da Pisa. He was released in 1299, became a wealthy merchant, married and had three children. He died in 1324 and was buried in the church of San Lorenzo in Venice.

The Travels of Marco Polo, also called Il Milione, was written down by Rustichello in Franco-Venetian as Devisement du Monde, probably as a handbook for merchants. There is no authoritative version, because the early manuscripts differ significantly, and about 150 copies in various languages are known. The first English translation, by John Frampton, was published in 1579.

Polo was not the first European in China, but he was the first to leave a detailed chronicle. He gave the first Western record of porcelain, gunpowder and paper money. Sceptics have pointed to omissions, such as the Great Wall, tea and chopsticks, and Frances Wood argued in 1995 that he went no farther than Persia. Supporters reply that the Great Wall known today is a Ming structure built two centuries later. His book inspired Christopher Columbus, who owned a copy with handwritten annotations.
marcus-aurelius: Marcus was born in Rome on 26 April 121, the son of the praetor Marcus Annius Verus, whose family came from Ucubi in Baetica, and of his wife. His father probably died in 125 or 126, and Marcus was raised by his grandfather Marcus Annius Verus, who held legal authority over him. In late 136 Hadrian chose Lucius Ceionius Commodus as his heir, apparently with the aim of eventually placing the young Marcus on the throne, but Commodus died in 138. Hadrian then adopted Antoninus Pius, who in turn adopted Marcus and Lucius, the son of Commodus. Marcus studied Greek and Latin under tutors including Herodes Atticus and Marcus Cornelius Fronto, and in 145 he married Antoninus's daughter Faustina.

After Antoninus died in 161 the Senate granted Marcus the name Augustus. He is said to have been compelled to take power, and his Stoic training made it clear that it was his duty. He soon betrothed his daughter Annia Lucilla to Lucius Verus, and the two emperors were popular for their lack of pomp. Marcus spent much of his time on law, giving particular attention to the manumission of slaves, the guardianship of orphans and minors, and the choice of city councillors; jurists called him an emperor most skilled in the law.

In late summer or early autumn of 161 Vologases IV of Parthia entered Armenia, then a Roman client state, and installed his own king. Marcus Sedatius Severianus, governor of Cappadocia, led a legion into Armenia and was trapped at Elegeia by the Parthian general Chosrhoes; he killed himself and his legion was massacred. The Parthian War lasted from 161 to 166. On the northern frontier the situation looked grave, with a frontier post destroyed and peoples of central and northern Europe in turmoil, and Marcus fought the Germanic tribes from 166 to 180. He reduced the silver purity of the denarius.

Persecution of Christians appears to have increased during his reign, though how far the emperor directed or knew of it is unclear and much debated by historians. He mentions Christians once in his Meditations, criticising what he saw as their theatrical approach to martyrdom.

Marcus died on 17 March 180, aged 58, of unknown causes, in his military quarters either at Vindobona or near Sirmium. He was deified at once, and his ashes were returned to Rome. His Meditations, written in Greek on campaign between 170 and 180 for his own guidance, is one of the most important sources for ancient Stoic philosophy. In Rome his bronze equestrian statue, made around 175 and the only Roman equestrian statue to survive, and his column, which celebrates his victory over the Sarmatians and Germanic tribes in 176, still stand.
margaret-thatcher: Margaret Hilda Roberts was born on 13 October 1925 in Grantham, Lincolnshire. Her father, Alfred Roberts, owned a tobacconist's and a grocery shop, served as an alderman and was a Methodist local preacher; he brought her up as a strict Wesleyan Methodist. She won a scholarship to Kesteven and Grantham Girls' School and entered Somerville College, Oxford, in October 1943 to study chemistry.

In 1950 and 1951 she was the Conservative candidate for the Labour seat of Dartford, losing both times. She married Denis Thatcher in December 1951 and qualified as a barrister in 1953. She was elected Member of Parliament for Finchley in 1959. Edward Heath appointed her Secretary of State for Education and Science in 1970, and in 1975 she defeated him in the Conservative Party leadership election, becoming the first woman to lead a major British political party.

Thatcher became prime minister on 4 May 1979. Her economic policies emphasised individual liberty, the privatisation of state-owned companies and reducing the power of trade unions. Her popularity waned during the recession and rising unemployment, but victory in the Falklands War in 1982 brought a resurgence of support and a landslide victory in 1983. In 1984 she survived the Provisional IRA's bombing of a Brighton hotel, and she achieved a political victory against the National Union of Mineworkers in the strike of 1984–85. In 1986 she oversaw the deregulation of financial markets known as the Big Bang.

She won a third term in 1987. Her support for the Community Charge, also called the poll tax, was widely unpopular, and her increasingly Eurosceptic views were not shared by others in her cabinet. After a challenge to her leadership she resigned in 1990 and was succeeded by John Major.

Thatcher retired from the House of Commons in 1992 and became Baroness Thatcher with a life peerage. She died of a stroke at the Ritz Hotel, London, on 8 April 2013, aged 87. Thatcherism was a systematic overhaul of the post-war consensus on Keynesianism, the welfare state, nationalised industry and high taxes. During her tenure the number of adults owning shares rose from 7 per cent to 25 per cent, and more than a million families bought their council houses. She remains a polarising figure, and the legacy of the shift towards neoliberal policies is still debated.
marie-antoinette: Maria Antonia Josepha Johanna was born on 2 November 1755 at the Hofburg Palace in Vienna, the fifteenth child and youngest daughter of Empress Maria Theresa and Francis I, Holy Roman Emperor. After the Seven Years' War, Maria Theresa ended her long hostility with Louis XV of France. Both wished to check the ambitions of Prussia and Great Britain, and they sealed the alliance with a marriage: on 7 February 1770 Louis XV formally asked for her hand for his grandson and heir, the Dauphin. When Louis XV died on 10 May 1774, the dauphin became Louis XVI and she became queen consort. Two weeks later the king gave her the Petit Trianon, a small château at Versailles.

As queen she became a target of those who opposed the policies of Louis XVI and of the monarchy in general. Libelles accused her of extravagance, promiscuity and sympathy for Austria. In 1785 members of her court defrauded jewellers in the Affair of the Diamond Necklace; she was falsely accused, but her reputation suffered. She was later called Madame Déficit, as the financial crisis was blamed on her spending and her opposition to reforms proposed by Turgot and Necker. In July 1789 she urged Necker's dismissal, and Paris rose to storm the Bastille.

In June 1791 the royal family tried to flee to Montmédy, the Flight to Varennes, which failed through poor execution. France declared war on Austria on 20 April 1792, and the queen was seen as an enemy. The attack on the Tuileries on 10 August 1792 forced the family to take refuge at the Legislative Assembly, and they were imprisoned in the Temple. The monarchy was abolished on 21 September, and Louis XVI was executed on 21 January 1793.

Marie Antoinette was moved to the Conciergerie, and a plot to free her failed in late August. Her trial before the Revolutionary Tribunal began on 14 October 1793; she and her lawyers had less than a day to prepare. The charges included sending millions of livres to Austria and incest, an accusation made by her son Louis-Charles under pressure from Jacques Hébert. She was convicted of high treason and guillotined on 16 October 1793. Her remains were exhumed in 1815, during the Bourbon Restoration, and buried at the Basilica of Saint-Denis. For many revolutionaries she symbolised the faults of the old regime.
mario-vargas-llosa: Mario Vargas Llosa was born to a middle-class family on 28 March 1936 in the southern Peruvian city of Arequipa. He was the only child of Ernesto Vargas Maldonado, a radio operator in an aviation company, and Dora Llosa Ureta, the daughter of an old criollo family. His parents separated a few months before his birth. His first literary influences were relatively obscure Peruvian writers such as Martín Adán, Carlos Oquendo de Amat and César Moro, from whom he sought new narrative structures to describe urban Peru.

His first novel, The Time of the Hero (1963), is set among cadets in a Lima military school and draws on his own experiences at the Leoncio Prado Military Academy. It won the Premio de la Crítica Española, and its sharp criticism of the Peruvian military led several generals to attack it. The Green House (1965) and Conversation in The Cathedral (1969), a two-volume novel based on the dictatorship of President Manuel A. Odría, followed. In 1971 he published a study of Gabriel García Márquez, his doctoral thesis for the Complutense University of Madrid; the two writers' friendship ended in 1976, when Vargas Llosa struck García Márquez at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City.

The War of the End of the World (1981) was his first historical novel, recreating the 19th-century War of Canudos in Brazil. He initially supported Fidel Castro's Cuban government, but broke with it over the imprisonment of the poet Heberto Padilla in 1971 and afterwards identified as a liberal. In 1983 he served on the commission investigating the Uchuraccay massacre, whose conclusions drew intense criticism from anthropologists. In 1987 he became a leader of the centre-right Movimiento Libertad, and in 1990 he ran for the presidency of Peru for the FREDEMO coalition, losing to Alberto Fujimori.

From the 1990s he lived mainly in Madrid and acquired Spanish citizenship in 1993. He received the Rómulo Gallegos Prize in 1967, the Prince of Asturias Award in 1986, the Miguel de Cervantes Prize in 1994 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2010. King Juan Carlos I made him Marquess of Vargas Llosa in 2011, and in 2021 he was elected to the Académie Française.

Vargas Llosa died in Lima on 13 April 2025, aged 89, surrounded by his family. His main theme was the individual's struggle for freedom within an oppressive reality, and he often challenged the inadequacies of society through his fiction. Scholars read his early novels as modernist and later ones such as Captain Pantoja and the Special Service as postmodernist and comic. He is counted among the major Latin American writers alongside Octavio Paz, Julio Cortázar, Jorge Luis Borges and Gabriel García Márquez.
mark-twain: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born on 30 November 1835 in Florida, Missouri, the sixth of seven children of Jane Lampton, a native of Kentucky, and John Marshall Clemens, a lawyer from Virginia. Only three of his siblings lived beyond childhood. When he was four the family moved to Hannibal, Missouri, a port town on the Mississippi River that inspired the fictional St. Petersburg of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn. Slavery was legal in Missouri at the time and became a theme in those books.

Twain became a riverboat pilot on the Mississippi, which gave him the material for Life on the Mississippi (1883). He then went west to join Orion in Nevada, joked about his failure at mining, and turned to journalism for the Virginia City Territorial Enterprise. A humorous story about a jumping frog of Calaveras County, published in 1865 and based on a tale he heard at the Angels Hotel in Angels Camp, California, brought him international attention. He became a much sought-after speaker.

His novels include The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876), Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889) and Pudd'nhead Wilson (1894), and he wrote The Gilded Age (1873) with Charles Dudley Warner. He began with light humorous verse and became a chronicler of the vanities, hypocrisies and murderous acts of mankind. In Huckleberry Finn he combined humor, narrative and social criticism, and he helped create a distinctive American literature built on American themes and language. The book has been repeatedly restricted in American high schools, not least for its frequent use of a racial slur.

His pen name, he said, came from the riverboatman's cry of mark twain, meaning that the water was two fathoms deep. He also said he took it from Captain Isaiah Sellers, who signed river news with it for the New Orleans Picayune. Some have doubted this story. His views became more radical with age, and he supported the labor movement, among others the Knights of Labor. He died of a heart attack on 21 April 1910, the day after Halley's Comet was closest to the Sun, as he had predicted.
marshall-islands: The Marshall Islands lie west of the International Date Line and north of the equator, about halfway between Hawaii and Australia, on the tops of ancient submerged volcanoes. The country consists of 29 atolls and five individual islands, and the atolls and islands form two roughly parallel chains running northwest to southeast, Ratak (sunrise) and Ralik (sunset). They cover about 1,900,000 square kilometres of ocean but only about 180 square kilometres of land, at an average height of 2.1 metres above sea level. The largest atoll by land area is Kwajalein, which surrounds a lagoon of about 1,700 square kilometres. Twenty-four of the atolls and islands are inhabited.

Austronesian settlers, possibly from the Solomon Islands, brought coconuts, giant swamp taro, breadfruit and domesticated chickens. Radiocarbon dates suggest Bikini Atoll may have been inhabited by 1200 BCE, though the samples are doubtful, and excavations on Majuro and Kwajalein show habitation around the 1st century CE. The wetter southern atolls probably held denser populations.

The first Europeans were the Spanish crew of Alonso de Salazar, who reached Taongi in 1526. European charts later named the group for the British captain John Marshall, who explored the region in 1788. American Protestant missionaries and Western traders arrived from the 1850s, and German copra traders dominated the economy in the 1870s and 1880s. After the First World War the islands became the Japanese South Seas Mandate. Under United States administration, 67 nuclear tests were conducted at Bikini and Enewetak between 1946 and 1958. In 1979 the United States recognised the Marshallese constitution and its president, Amata Kabua.

The capital and largest city is Majuro, where about half of the population lives; the 2021 census counted 42,418 residents. Marshallese and English are the official languages. The country is a presidential parliamentary republic in free association with the United States, with a legislature called the Nitijela and an advisory Council of Iroij of twelve paramount chiefs. Land is the main measure of a family's wealth and is inherited through the maternal line. Some 96.2 per cent of people identified with a Christian denomination at the 2021 census, the largest being the United Church of Christ - Congregational in the Marshall Islands.
martin-luther: Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 to Hans Luder and his wife Margarethe in Eisleben. In 1484 the family moved to Mansfeld, where his father leased copper mines and smelters and later became a town councillor. Hans was determined that his eldest son should become a lawyer. Luther entered the University of Erfurt in 1501 and received his master's degree in 1505, but dropped out of law almost at once. According to one story, a lightning bolt struck near him during a thunderstorm on 2 July 1505, and he cried out, "Help! Saint Anna, I will become a monk!" He entered St Augustine's Monastery in Erfurt on 17 July 1505, to his father's fury.

As an Augustinian friar Luther devoted himself to fasting, prayer and confession, and described this period as one of deep spiritual despair. He was ordained on 3 April 1507, began teaching theology at the University of Wittenberg in 1508 and received his Doctor of Theology on 19 October 1512, succeeding Johann von Staupitz as chair of theology.

From 1510 to 1520 he lectured on the Psalms, Hebrews, Romans and Galatians, and became convinced that the Church was corrupt. The most important doctrine for him was justification by faith alone through God's grace, which he held to be entirely God's work. He taught that the Bible is the only source of divinely revealed knowledge of the Gospel, which challenged the authority of the pope and bishops. Pope Leo X excommunicated him in January 1521, and that year Emperor Charles V condemned him as an outlaw at the Diet of Worms.

At Luther's death in 1546 his excommunication was still in effect. He made effective use of the printing press and wrote in German to reach a broader audience; between 1500 and 1530 his works made up one fifth of all materials printed in Germany. His German Bible of 1534 fostered a standard version of the German language, and his marriage to Katharina von Bora, a former nun, set a model for clerical marriage.

Luther expressed staunchly antisemitic views, calling for the expulsion of Jews and the burning of synagogues. According to the prevailing opinion among historians, his anti-Jewish rhetoric contributed significantly to the development of antisemitism in Germany, and Nazi propaganda cited it.
martin-luther-king-jr: Martin Luther King Jr. was born Michael King Jr. on 15 January 1929 in Atlanta, the second of three children of Michael King and Alberta King. His maternal grandfather, Adam Daniel Williams, was a minister who became pastor of the Ebenezer Baptist Church. King enrolled at Crozer Theological Seminary in Pennsylvania, where he was elected president of the student body, and later studied at Boston University. He married Coretta Scott on 18 June 1953.

King oversaw the 1955 Montgomery bus boycott, was the first president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, helped organise the 1963 protests in Birmingham, Alabama, and was one of the leaders of the 1963 March on Washington, where he gave the I Have a Dream speech. On 14 October 1964 he became the youngest winner of the Nobel Peace Prize. The FBI director J. Edgar Hoover ordered surveillance of him, and a 1975 congressional investigation found that from December 1963 until his death he was the target of an intensive campaign to neutralise him.

In March 1968 King went to Memphis, Tennessee, to support striking black sanitation workers, and on 3 April gave the address I've Been to the Mountaintop. He was assassinated on 4 April 1968. James Earl Ray was convicted of the killing, though conspiracy theories persist, and King's death led to riots in American cities. Martin Luther King Jr. Day was first observed as a federal holiday in 1986.
mary-mother-of-jesus: Mary was a first-century Jewish woman of Nazareth, the wife of Joseph and the mother of Jesus. The canonical Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles are the primary sources, and they give limited information because they focus on the teaching of Jesus and his apostles. They are generally dated to about 66–110 CE, and their historical reliability is debated. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke describe Mary as a virgin chosen by God to conceive Jesus through the Holy Spirit. After the birth in Bethlehem, she and Joseph raised him in Nazareth in Galilee, and she was in Jerusalem at his crucifixion.

Apocryphal texts add details, such as the Gospel of James, which names her parents as Joachim and Anne and says she was given to the Temple in Jerusalem at the age of three. Scholars generally consider such texts mainly unreliable. In the 2nd century the pagan philosopher Celsus claimed that Jesus was the illegitimate son of a Roman soldier named Panthera, and the Church Father Origen dismissed this as a fabrication.

The Bible does not describe the end of Mary's life. Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and some Oriental Orthodox and Protestant traditions hold that her body was raised into heaven at its close, which Western Christianity calls the Assumption and Eastern Christianity the Dormition of the Mother of God. The Catholic Church also holds the dogma of her Immaculate Conception.

Mary has been venerated since early Christianity. Eastern and Oriental Orthodox, Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches hold that she is the Mother of God, while many Protestants pay far less attention to her. Devotion takes the form of prayers and hymns, feast days, the veneration of images and relics, churches and pilgrimages. In Islam, where she is called Maryam, she has the highest position among women, and a chapter of the Quran is named for her. She is also revered in the Druze and Bahá'í faiths. In Western art she is traditionally painted in blue, a custom that goes back to the Byzantine Empire.
mary-shelley: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in Somers Town, London, on 30 August 1797, the child of the philosopher William Godwin and the women's rights advocate Mary Wollstonecraft, who died of puerperal fever eleven days after the birth. Godwin brought her up with her older half-sister, Fanny Imlay, gave her a rich informal education and encouraged her in his own anarchist political theories. When she was four, he married a neighbour, Mary Jane Clairmont, with whom Mary had a troubled relationship.

In 1814 she began a romance with Percy Bysshe Shelley, a follower of her father who was already married. With her stepsister Claire Clairmont they left for France and travelled through Europe. After their return they faced ostracism, constant debt and the death of their daughter. Percy's wife Harriet was found drowned in December 1816, and Mary and Percy married on 30 December.

In May 1816 the couple and Claire Clairmont went to Geneva to spend the summer with Lord Byron, who rented the Villa Diodati with his physician John William Polidori. There Mary conceived the idea for Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, published in 1818. How far Percy contributed to it is argued: James Rieger saw him as editor or minor collaborator, while Anne K. Mellor held that he only made technical corrections.

The Shelleys left Britain for Italy in 1818. Two of their children died there, and Percy Florence was born on 12 November 1819. In 1822 Percy drowned when his boat sank in a storm near Viareggio, and a year later she returned to England as a professional author. Her novels include Valperga, The Last Man (1826), Lodore and Falkner, and she wrote biographies for Dionysius Lardner's Cabinet Cyclopaedia between 1832 and 1839. She published Percy's Posthumous Poems in 1824 and a new edition of his poetry in 1839.

The last decade of her life was dogged by illness, most likely caused by the brain tumour that killed her at the age of 53, on 1 February 1851. Until the 1970s she was known mainly for Frankenstein and her efforts to publish her husband's works. Recent scholarship finds in her other writing a political radical who argued that cooperation and sympathy, as practised by women in the family, were the ways to reform society.
mary-wollstonecraft: Mary Wollstonecraft was born on 27 April 1759 in Spitalfields, London, the second of the seven children of Elizabeth Dixon and Edward John Wollstonecraft. The family had a comfortable income in her childhood, but her father gradually squandered it on speculative projects, and the family moved often. He was apparently a violent man who beat his wife in drunken rages, and as a teenager Wollstonecraft lay outside her mother's bedroom door to protect her. She played a similar maternal role for her sisters Everina and Eliza. In 1784 she arranged for Eliza, probably suffering from postpartum depression, to leave her husband and infant, a decision that brought her sister social condemnation and poverty.

After Blood's death in 1785, Wollstonecraft's friends helped her to a post as governess to the daughters of the Anglo-Irish Kingsborough family in Ireland. Her early writings concern education, among them Thoughts on the Education of Daughters (1787), the children's book Original Stories from Real Life (1788) and the anthology The Female Reader. She also translated children's works. Her first novel, Mary: A Fiction, appeared in 1788, and her unfinished Maria: or, The Wrongs of Woman was published after her death in 1798. Both novels criticise marriage and its effects on women.

A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790) answered Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, attacking aristocracy and advocating republicanism. It was the first reply in what became known as the Revolution Controversy. Wollstonecraft left for Paris in December 1792, shortly before Louis XVI was guillotined, and associated mostly with the moderate Girondins. There she fell in love with the American adventurer Gilbert Imlay, and their daughter Fanny was born. She was disillusioned by what she saw, writing that the new government remained venal and brutal. She wrote An Historical and Moral View of the French Revolution (1794).

Imlay rejected her when she returned to London in April 1795, and she attempted suicide twice. She travelled to Scandinavia on his business and recounted the journey in Letters Written in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark (1796). She later married the philosopher William Godwin.

Wollstonecraft gave birth to her second daughter, Mary, on 30 August 1797 and died of septicaemia on 10 September, at the age of 38. The daughter became the author of Frankenstein. Godwin's Memoirs of 1798 revealed her love affairs, illegitimate children and suicide attempts, and the Romantic poet Robert Southey accused him of stripping his dead wife naked. Her reputation lay in tatters for nearly a century, and novelists such as Maria Edgeworth pilloried her in their characters. With the feminist movement at the turn of the twentieth century her advocacy of women's equality was increasingly recognised.
maryland: Maryland borders Virginia to the south, West Virginia to the west, Pennsylvania to the north and Delaware to the east, as well as the Atlantic Ocean to the east and Washington, D.C. to the southwest. With an area of 12,407 square miles (32,130 km2) it is the ninth-smallest state by land area. The western portion contains stretches of the Appalachian Mountains, the centre is mainly Piedmont, and the east takes in a large part of the Chesapeake Bay, which nearly bisects the state.

The variety of its landscape, from sandy dunes in the east to marshes near the bay, oak forests in the Piedmont and pine groves in the mountains, has earned it the nickname America in Miniature. Its history as a border state has left it with traits of both North and South.

Present-day Maryland was inhabited by Native peoples, mostly Algonquian, including the Piscataway, the Nanticoke and the Susquehannock. George Calvert, 1st Baron Baltimore, sought a charter from King Charles I for the territory between Massachusetts and Virginia. After he died in April 1632, the charter was granted to his son Cecilius Calvert, 2nd Baron Baltimore, on 20 June 1632. The colony was named in honour of Henrietta Maria of France, wife of Charles I.

The land was first settled in 1634, primarily to provide a religious haven for Catholics persecuted in England. Religious strife was common in the early years, and Catholics remained a minority, though in greater numbers than in any other English colony. The original capital was St. Mary's City on the north shore of the Potomac River. The economy was plantation-based and centred on tobacco, and demand for cheap labour led to the importation of many indentured servants and enslaved Africans.

Maryland's current boundaries took form in 1760, after the settlement of a long-running border dispute with Pennsylvania. Georgetown, Maryland, and other land from Montgomery and Prince George's counties was ceded to the federal government in 1790 to form Washington, D.C. Although Maryland was a slave state, it remained in the Union during the American Civil War, in part because Abraham Lincoln left the National Guard there.

The capital is Annapolis and the most populous city is Baltimore. The 2020 census counted 6,185,278 residents. Its nearness to Washington, D.C. shapes its economy, which includes defense, biotechnology and higher education, and the state hosts some of the highest numbers of historic landmarks per capita.
maseru: Maseru lies in north-western Lesotho, directly on the border with South Africa, which is marked by the Mohokare, or Caledon, River. A border post at the Maseru Bridge connects the two countries, and the nearest town on the South African side is Ladybrand. The city sits in a shallow valley at the foot of the Hlabeng-Sa-Likhama, foothills of the Maloti Mountains, at about 1,600 metres above sea level. It has a subtropical highland climate with warm, rainy summers and cool to chilly, dry winters. The name is a Sesotho word meaning red sandstones.

The British founded Maseru as a small police camp in 1869, after the end of the Free State–Basotho Wars, when Basutoland became a British protectorate. It stands at the edge of the conquered territories relinquished to the Orange Free State under the peace terms, 24 kilometres west of King Moshoeshoe I's stronghold of Thaba Bosiu, the previous de facto capital. A busy market town soon grew around the camp.

Maseru served as the administrative capital from 1869 to 1871, before administration passed to the Cape Colony. During Cape rule from 1871 to 1884 Basutoland was treated like forcibly annexed territory, which led to the Gun War of 1881 and the burning of many buildings in Maseru. In 1884 Basutoland was restored to the status of a Crown colony and Maseru became the capital again. It stayed small under British rule, which took little interest in developing it. After independence in 1966 its area grew about sevenfold, from around 20 to 138 square kilometres, as nearby villages were incorporated, and its population grew by around 7% a year for several decades. Riots after the 1998 parliamentary elections damaged much of the city.

Maseru is the capital and largest city of Lesotho and of Maseru District, and the 2016 census counted 330,760 people, about one seventh of the country's population. Traditional thatched mud-brick rondavels have largely given way to modern buildings. Colonial-era buildings include the Roman Catholic Cathedral of Our Lady of Victories and the Anglican St. John's Church, and the city also has the Royal Palace, the Parliament building and the State House. Kingsway, which joins the Royal Palace and the airport, was the first paved road in Lesotho. The national stadium, Setsoto Stadium, is in the city.
matsuo-basho: Matsuo Bashō was born Matsuo Kinsaku in 1644 near Ueno, in Iga Province. The Matsuo family was of samurai descent, and his father was probably a musokunin, one of a class of landowning peasants with certain samurai privileges. In his late teens he became a servant, in a humble capacity, to Tōdō Yoshitada, with whom he shared a love of haikai no renga, a form of collaborative poetry. A sequence opened with a verse of 5-7-5 mora called a hokku, later renamed haiku when it stood alone.

Yoshitada's sudden death in 1666 ended Bashō's peaceful life, and he is believed to have given up any chance of samurai status. By 1680 he taught twenty disciples in Edo, and that winter he moved to Fukagawa, where his disciples built him a hut and planted a banana tree, bashō in Japanese, which gave him his pen name.

In 1684 he left Edo on the first of four major journeys, travelling alone on routes regarded as dangerous. His poems grew less introspective, and in early 1686 he composed the hokku about an ancient pond and a frog jumping in, which was at once widely praised.

On 16 May 1689 he left Edo with his student Kawai Sora for the Northern Provinces of Honshū, a journey of 600 ri, about 2,400 km, that became his masterwork Oku no Hosomichi, The Narrow Road to the Deep North. He edited it for three years, and the first edition appeared posthumously in 1702. It was an immediate commercial success and other itinerant poets followed his route. Bashō himself believed his best work lay in leading and joining renku.

In 1693 he adopted karumi, or lightness, a semi-Buddhist philosophy of greeting the mundane world instead of separating from it. In the summer of 1694 he left Edo for the last time and in Osaka fell ill with a stomach complaint, dying peacefully on 28 November 1694 among his disciples. In 1793 the Shinto bureaucracy deified him, so that for a time criticising his poetry was blasphemous. Masaoka Shiki challenged this orthodoxy in the late 19th century, yet also made Bashō accessible in English and coined the term haiku.
mattavilasa-prahasana: The play opens with two drunken Kapalikas, the mendicant Satyasoma and his partner Devasoma, stumbling from tavern to tavern in search of more liquor. The Kapalikas are presented as followers of a heretical Saivite sect whose rites included drinking, wild dancing and singing, and ritual intercourse. Asking for alms, Satyasoma finds that his skull-bowl is gone. It is not at the tavern they last visited, and he suspects that either a dog or a Buddhist monk has taken it.

A Buddhist monk named Nagasena then enters, and Satyasoma accuses him of the theft. He charges the monk with stealing, lying and desiring liquor, meat and women although his religion forbids them, and accuses Buddhism itself of stealing ideas from the Mahabharata and the Vedanta. The monk denies everything and the quarrel becomes a brawl, which a Pasupata acquaintance of Satyasoma tries to mediate. In despair the monk hands over his own begging bowl. At last a Madman comes on stage carrying the real skull-bowl, which he has recovered from a dog; it is returned to its owner and all leave on friendly terms.

The play was written during a strong revival of Hinduism in southern India, which Mahendravarman I supported; he had temples cut into the rock, most of them dedicated to Siva. It is widely held to be a satire on sects that seemed degenerate or peculiar in his day. The Kapalikas stood for Tantrism, in which enlightenment was sought through unorthodox rituals involving liquor and ritual intercourse; the monk, in turn, wonders why Buddhism forbids liquor and women, and both Kapalikas call the Jains heretics.

The text also gives a view of life in seventh-century Kanchipuram, with references to the sound of drums, flower shops, festive taverns, temple towers and courts whose officials were sometimes bribed. English translations include those of Michael Lockwood and A. Vishnu Bhat, of 1981, and David Lorenzen, of 2001. A dance-theatre adaptation directed by Stella Uppal-Subbiah, which gave prominence to bharatanatyam, toured the United Kingdom in 2003 and 2004.
mauritania: Mauritania lies in the western region of Africa and is generally flat, its 1,030,000 square kilometres forming vast, arid plains broken by occasional ridges and clifflike outcroppings. It borders the Atlantic Ocean, Senegal, Mali, Algeria and Western Sahara, and is considered part of both the Sahel and the Maghreb. Approximately three-quarters of the country is desert or semidesert, and the desert has been expanding since the mid-1960s after extended, severe drought. The highest of its sandstone plateaus, the Adrar Plateau, reaches 500 metres, and the concentric Guelb er Richat is a prominent feature of the north-central region.

The name comes from Mauretania, the Latin name of an ancient Berber kingdom and later Roman province that lay considerably farther north, along the western Mediterranean coast of Africa. The territories do not overlap. Arab geographers more commonly called the land Bilad Chinqit, the land of Chinguetti. The French officially used the term Mauritanie occidentale in 1899, on a proposal by the colonial administrator Xavier Coppolani.

The ancient tribes of Mauritania were the Niger-Congo and Bafour peoples. The Bafour were among the first Saharan peoples to abandon a nomadic lifestyle for agriculture, and migrated southward as the Sahara dried. They were displaced by Berbers who arrived between the 3rd and 7th centuries. The Umayyads were the first Arab Muslims to enter the region, establishing themselves by the end of the 7th century. In the 11th century several Berber confederations in the desert joined to form the Almoravid movement, which built an empire stretching from the Sahara to the Iberian Peninsula.

From 1644 to 1674 the indigenous peoples made a final, unsuccessful effort to repel the Maqil Arabs, led by the Beni Hassan tribe, in the Char Bouba War. The descendants of the Beni Hassan warriors became the upper stratum of Moorish society, and Hassaniya, a bedouin Arabic dialect named for them, became the dominant language of the largely nomadic population. In the early 20th century France colonised the country as part of French West Africa. It became independent in 1960.

Mauritania is the Islamic Republic of Mauritania. Its capital and largest city is Nouakchott, on the Atlantic coast, and its population is about 5 million. Arabic is the official language, with Pulaar, Soninke and Wolof as national languages, and Islam is the state religion. Its manuscript libraries at Chinguetti hold thousands of medieval manuscripts, and it has a long oral tradition of poetry.
mauritius: The main island lies 1,100 nautical miles (2,000 km) off the southeast coast of Africa, between latitudes 19°58.8'S and 20°31.7'S. It is 65 km long and 45 km wide. It is geologically young, created by volcanic activity some 8 million years ago, and with Réunion, Rodrigues and Saint Brandon it forms part of the Mascarene Islands, which are no longer volcanically active. White sandy beaches surround it, and lagoons are protected by a coral reef. The country also includes Rodrigues, Agaléga and St. Brandon. The main island was the only known home of the dodo, which became extinct soon after human settlement.

The island was uninhabited when first visited. Some historians have speculated from the Cantino planisphere of 1502, where it appears as Dina Arobi, that Arab sailors reached it around 975. Portuguese sailors visited in 1507, and Diogo Fernandes Pereira is the first European known to have landed; the Portuguese did not stay. A Dutch squadron under Admiral Wybrand Van Warwyck landed at Grand Port in 1598 and named the island after Prince Maurice of Nassau. The Dutch inhabited it from 1638, exploiting ebony trees and introducing sugar cane, domestic animals and deer.

French colonisation began in 1715, and the island was renamed Isle de France. In 1810 the United Kingdom seized it, and France ceded Mauritius and its dependencies in the Treaty of Paris. The British colony included Rodrigues, Agaléga, St. Brandon, the Chagos Archipelago and, until 1906, the Seychelles. Mauritius became the British Empire's main sugar-producing colony and stayed a plantation colony dominated by sugar until independence in 1968. The country became a republic in 1992.

In 1965, three years before independence, the United Kingdom split the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius to form the British Indian Ocean Territory, established on 8 November 1965. The local population was forcibly expelled, and the main island, Diego Garcia, was leased to the United States for a military base.

Mauritius is a parliamentary republic with a unicameral National Assembly, and its capital and largest city is Port Louis. Its people are diverse in ethnicity, culture, language and faith, drawn from Indian, African, Chinese and European, mostly French, origins. It is the only country in Africa where Hinduism is the most practised religion. Its architecture combines Dutch, French and British styles with influences from India and East Africa.
max-weber: Maximilian Carl Emil Weber was born on 21 April 1864 in Erfurt and raised in Charlottenburg, the oldest of eight children. His father, Max Weber Sr., was a lawyer, civil servant and National Liberal parliamentarian, and the family's salon welcomed scholars such as the historian Theodor Mommsen. His mother, Helene Fallenstein, was a devout Calvinist and philanthropist. He studied law and history in Berlin, Göttingen and Heidelberg, took his doctorate in law in 1889 and his habilitation in 1891, and in 1893 married his second cousin Marianne Schnitger, a feminist activist and author.

Weber taught in Berlin, Freiburg and Heidelberg. In 1897 he suffered a breakdown after his father died following an argument, and he ceased teaching and travelled for several years. From 1904 he was an associate editor of the Archiv für Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik, in which he published The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism.

He first supported Germany's war effort in 1914 but became a prominent critic of expansionism and of the Kaiser's war policies, and he called for democratisation. After the war he co-founded the German Democratic Party, advised on the drafting of the Weimar Constitution, and taught in Vienna and Munich, where he gave the lectures Science as a Vocation and Politics as a Vocation. He died of pneumonia on 14 June 1920, possibly as a result of the Spanish flu.

A central concern was rationalisation and disenchantment. In The Protestant Ethic he argued that Protestantism, particularly Calvinism, tied piety to a worldly calling and so encouraged rational economic gain. He later studied the religions of China, India and ancient Judaism. He defined the state by its monopoly on the legitimate use of force within a given area, and divided legitimate authority into traditional, charismatic and rational-legal forms.

Methodologically he placed social action at the centre of sociology, sought to understand it through interpretation, and used ideal types as models to compare with reality. Economy and Society was left unfinished. He is now regarded alongside Karl Marx and Émile Durkheim as a founding figure of sociology.
maximilien-robespierre: Robespierre was baptised on 6 May 1758 in Arras, in Artois, the eldest of four children of François Maximilien Barthélémy de Robespierre, a lawyer, and Jacqueline Marguerite Carrault, the daughter of a brewer. After three years of law studies he graduated in July 1780 with a special prize for academic achievement and conduct. Admitted to the bar, he was appointed one of the five judges of the local criminal court in March 1782, but soon resigned, uncomfortable at passing capital sentences because he opposed the death penalty.

In the Estates General he gave his first speech on 6 June 1789, attacking the hierarchy of the church. In 1790 he demanded that all Frenchmen be admissible to public positions without distinction other than virtue and talent, and on 31 March was elected president of the Jacobin Club. In 1791 he gave 328 speeches and argued that all citizens, not only those with the vote, should be allowed to serve in the National Guard. He warned the Jacobins against war with Austria, saying on 2 January 1792 that no one loves armed missionaries.

He was elected to the National Convention in September 1792, where the Jacobins sat on the high benches known as the Mountain, and he worked to bring about the execution of Louis XVI, who was guillotined on 21 January 1793.

On 27 July 1793 Robespierre joined the Committee of Public Safety, at a time when France faced rebellion in the Vendée and in Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux and hostility across Europe. In a report of 5 February 1794 he argued that in revolution the springs of popular government were virtue and terror together. Danton and Desmoulins were tried in April 1794. The Law of 22 Prairial, passed on 10 June, denied accused persons counsel and left the revolutionary tribunals only two verdicts, acquittal or death; within three days 156 people were sent to the guillotine. On 6 and 7 May 1794 he had announced the recognition of God and the immortality of the soul and the festivals of the Supreme Being.

On 9 Thermidor, almost thirty-five deputies, most of them from the Mountain, spoke against Robespierre, and his voice was shouted down. He was arrested with around 90 others, among them Louis Antoine de Saint-Just, Georges Couthon and his brother Augustin. On 28 July 1794 he and twenty-one others were condemned under the Law of 22 Prairial without a hearing and guillotined. The Thermidorians held him the most culpable for the bloodshed, and Lazare Carnot called him a hypocrite. His views and policies remain controversial: he is remembered for his campaigns for the voting rights of all men and against the Atlantic slave trade, and for his part in the repression of the Revolution's opponents.
may-coup-poland: Józef Piłsudski had largely controlled the politics of the re-established Polish state but lost that advantage after the failed Kiev offensive of spring 1920, while keeping the esteem of parts of the armed forces. In November 1925 the cabinet of Władysław Grabski gave way to that of Aleksander Skrzyński, backed by the National Democrats and the Polish Socialist Party; when the socialists withdrew, it fell in turn and was replaced by a government under Wincenty Witos, formed by the Polish People's Party "Piast" and the Christian Union of National Unity. It had even less popular support than its predecessors.

Piłsudski regarded the constant shifts of power in the Sejm, the Polish parliament, as chaotic and damaging. He also saw threats to Poland's independence in the Locarno Treaties of 1925, by which the western but not the eastern borders of Germany were guaranteed, and in the Treaty of Berlin concluded by Germany and the Soviet Union in 1926.

On 10 May 1926, the day the Witos government was formed, Piłsudski told the newspaper Kurier Poranny that he was ready to fight the evil of sejmocracy, a contemptuous word for rule by parliament, and promised a sanation, or restoration to health, of political life. The edition was confiscated. In the night of 11–12 May units of the Warsaw garrison marched to Rembertów and pledged him their support; on 12 May they moved on Warsaw and took the bridges over the Vistula River.

At about 17:00 Piłsudski met President Stanisław Wojciechowski on the Poniatowski Bridge. He demanded the resignation of the cabinet; the president demanded that his forces capitulate. Fighting began at about 19:00. On 14 May the Polish Socialist Party declared for the rebels and called a general strike, and striking railwaymen kept government reinforcements from reaching Warsaw. To prevent a nationwide civil war, Wojciechowski and Witos resigned. In all 215 soldiers and 164 civilians were killed and some 900 people wounded.

Kazimierz Bartel formed a new government with Piłsudski as minister of military affairs. On 31 May the National Assembly nominated Piłsudski as president, but he declined, and Ignacy Mościcki took the office. Piłsudski held the posts of defence minister and inspector general of the armed forces in every government until his death, and headed two of them himself, in 1926–1928 and 1930. In 1935 his supporters replaced the democratic March Constitution with the April Constitution, which provided for a strong presidency but came too late for him to assume it.
mbabane: Mbabane lies on the Mbabane River and its tributary the Polinjane River in the Mdzimba Mountains, at an average elevation of 1,243 metres. It is in the Hhohho Region, of which it is also the capital. Because of its altitude it has a moderate subtropical highland climate: snow is rare, having fallen only three times since 1900, and the city averages only four days of frost a year. Most of the rain falls in summer. The city takes its name from a chief, Mbabane Kunene, who lived in the area when British settlers arrived.

The town stands at the spot where the route from the Transvaal to Mozambique crossed the Mbabane River. It grew after the administrative centre of the country was moved from Bremersdorp, now called Manzini, in January 1902, and Great Britain declared it the capital of the new Protectorate of Swaziland that year. At that time it consisted of a few shops, churches and schools founded by white settlers, and Swazi Africans were not allowed to live in the town but had to reside in nearby rural districts. By the 1930s it had electricity, running water, a telephone connection and a hospital.

Before World War II most Swazis lived in rural districts and worked outside the country, so there was little growth in the town. After the war, the creation of trade schools in the city, the arrival of the Goba railway connecting Maputo to the mines in South Africa and Lesotho, and foreign investment, particularly in the sugar industry, contributed to its growth. In the years following independence government buildings were built in Mbabane, among them the British Consulate.

Mbabane is the most populous city of Eswatini, previously called Swaziland, with an estimated population of 94,874 in 2010. It is one of the two capitals, the executive capital, alongside Lobamba. The main language is siSwati, and English is widely spoken. Tin and iron were mined nearby, and the city is a commercial and financial hub for the surrounding region and a centre of the country's tourism. It is home to Waterford-Kamhlaba United World College of Southern Africa and one of the three campuses of the University of Eswatini.
measles: Measles is a vaccine-preventable infectious disease caused by the measles virus, an RNA virus closely related to rinderpest, which affects cattle, and to canine distemper. Symptoms usually appear 10 to 12 days after exposure and last 7 to 10 days. They begin with fever, often above 40 °C (104 °F), cough, a runny nose and inflamed eyes, followed by a rash that starts on the face and spreads to the rest of the body.

The disease spreads through the air in the coughs and sneezes of infected people. Common complications include diarrhoea in 8 per cent of cases, middle ear infection in 7 per cent and pneumonia in 6 per cent, in part because measles weakens the immune system. Immunity is lifelong once acquired, through vaccination or after recovery.

Measles is of zoonotic origin: it evolved from rinderpest. Genomic analysis indicates that it arose as a human disease between 900 and 2,400 years ago. The Antonine Plague of 165 to 180 CE has been suggested as measles, but its cause is unknown and smallpox is thought more likely.

The first systematic description of measles as distinct from smallpox and chickenpox is credited to the Persian physician Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (860 to 932), who wrote The Book of Smallpox and Measles. Between 1100 and 1200 CE the virus is thought to have diverged completely from rinderpest. This fits the observation that measles needs a susceptible population of over 500,000 to sustain an epidemic, a size reached in historic times with the growth of medieval European cities.

Before vaccination, measles was endemic in every part of the world. In 1954 John Enders and Thomas C. Peebles isolated the virus from a 13-year-old boy in the United States, David Edmonston. Enders grew the Edmonston strain in human kidney tissue, then in amniotic membrane and finally in chick embryo culture, producing over three years a virus that gave immunity without causing disease, a process called attenuation.

At Merck, Maurice Hilleman attenuated the strain further, and the first successful measles vaccine became widely available in the United States in 1963. Measles vaccine was later combined with those for mumps and rubella as the MMR vaccine, licensed in the United States in 1971.
mecca: Mecca, officially Makkah al-Mukarramah, lies in the Hejaz region of western Arabia, about 70 kilometres inland from Jeddah, in a narrow valley 277 metres above sea level. The city centres on the Masjid al-Haram, the Great Mosque, which contains the Kaaba. Muslims believe the Kaaba was built by Abraham and Ishmael. It is the direction of prayer (qibla) for all Muslims. The mosque is also the site of the Zamzam Well and of two rites of the Hajj and the Umrah, the circumambulation of the Kaaba (tawaf) and the walk between Safa and Marwa.

The early history of Mecca is poorly documented. The city lies in the interior of western Arabia, where few textual or archaeological sources survive, in contrast to Yemen and the Syro-Palestinian frontier. One study, by Majied Robinson, based on early Islamic genealogical records, estimates the population at the time of Muhammad at about 550, while Muslim scholars using traditional sources may place it as high as 10,000. One proposed etymology links the name to an Old South Arabian root meaning temple.

Muslim rulers from in and around the region long tried to control the city. The first printing press came to Mecca in 1885 with the Ottoman governor Osman Nuri Pasha. The city was last conquered in 1925, in the Saudi conquest of the Hejaz by Ibn Saud and his allies. Non-Muslims are forbidden to enter. The first recorded outsider to do so was Ludovico di Varthema of Bologna in 1503; Guru Nanak is said to have visited in December 1518, and Richard Francis Burton entered in 1853 disguised as a Qadiriyya Sufi from Afghanistan.

Mecca is the capital of Mecca Province in Saudi Arabia, and its metropolitan population was 2.4 million in 2022. Pilgrims on the Hajj, observed in the twelfth Hijri month of Dhū al-Ḥijjah as an obligation on Muslims once in their lives, more than triple that number each year. Mecca's economy depends heavily on pilgrimage. In the 20th century it expanded greatly, and several historical structures, among them the Ajyad Fortress, were demolished, in part for the enlargement of the Masjid al-Haram.
mecklenburg-vorpommern: The state covers 23,300 km2, the sixth largest German state by area. Its Baltic coastline of about 2,000 km has peninsulas, lagoons and islands, among them Germany's two biggest, Rügen and Usedom. In the south lies the Mecklenburg Lake District, where Lake Müritz is the largest lake in Germany. The name Vorpommern comes from West Slavic po more, land at the sea, with the German prefix vor- meaning the nearer part of Pomerania.

Human settlement began after the Ice Age, about 10,000 BCE. Germanic peoples recorded there about two thousand years ago mostly left during the Migration Period, and from the sixth century Polabian Slavs settled the area: the Obotrites in Mecklenburg, the Veleti and Rani in Pomerania. Vikings and Slavs set up trading posts along the coast, such as Reric, Ralswiek and Menzlin. In the late 12th century Henry the Lion, Duke of the Saxons, conquered the Obotrites and Christianized them, and German settlers followed in the Ostsiedlung. Mecklenburg became a duchy of the Holy Roman Empire in 1348 and its two grand duchies of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz were created in 1815.

The Duchy of Pomerania was a vassal state of Poland from 1121 to 1138, and its dukes were later vassals of Saxony, the Holy Roman Empire and Denmark before staying with the Empire from 1227. Western Pomerania was under Swedish rule from the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 until 1815 and then became part of the Prussian Province of Pomerania, remaining so until 1945.

The Soviet military administration created the Province of Mecklenburg and West Pomerania on 9 July 1945, by order of Marshal Georgy Zhukov. Expellees from the former eastern territories of Germany raised the population by 40%, and in 1949 they made up 43.3% of it. The state's name was shortened to Land Mecklenburg in 1947, and it became a constituent state of the German Democratic Republic in 1949. In 1952 it was divided into the districts of Rostock, Schwerin and Neubrandenburg. At reunification in 1990 the state was re-established along its postwar boundaries under the name Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

Schwerin is the state capital, and Rostock, with about 205,000 inhabitants, is the largest city. The University of Rostock, founded in 1419, and the University of Greifswald, founded in 1456, are among the oldest in Europe. The old Hanseatic towns of Stralsund and Wismar are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and red Brick Gothic churches and houses are a feature of many towns.
medellin: Medellín lies in the Aburrá Valley, a central region of the Andes in northwestern South America, at an elevation of about 1,500 m. The Medellín River, also called the Porce, flows northward through the valley. Because of its altitude the climate is milder than at other places at the same latitude, with an average temperature of 22 °C that varies little through the year, and the city is known as the City of the Eternal Spring.

In August 1541 Marshal Jorge Robledo saw what he took to be a valley, and Jerónimo Luis Tejelo reached the plain of the Aburrá Valley on the night of 23 August. The Spaniards called it the Valley of Saint Bartholomew, but the name soon gave way to the native name Aburrá, Painters, for the textile decorations of the local rulers. The valley lay between the gold mines northeast of Antioquia and the first provincial capital, Santa Fe de Antioquia, and supplied food to the mines.

In 1616 Francisco de Herrera Campuzano set up a small indigenous village, San Lorenzo de Aburrá, in what is now El Poblado. On 2 November 1675 the queen consort Mariana of Austria founded the Town of Our Lady of Candelaria of Medellín in the Aná region, now the city centre. In 1826 Gran Colombia's National Congress named the city capital of the Department of Antioquia. During the 19th century it was a commercial centre, first exporting gold, then coffee.

In the first half of the 20th century the population grew sixfold, from 59,815 in 1905 to 358,189 in 1951. The Coltejer textile company was founded in 1907 by Alejandro Echavarría. After the murder of the presidential candidate Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in 1948, political violence spread in the countryside, farmers fled to the cities and the valley slopes filled with slums. The city later built the Medellín Metro.

Medellín is the capital of Antioquia and the second-largest city in Colombia after Bogotá, with 2,427,129 people at the 2018 census. The University of Antioquia, the National University of Colombia's Medellín branch and the Pontifical Bolivarian University have long been its academic centres. Little colonial architecture remains; the Candelaria Church and the Church of the Veracruz survive, much altered. The Museum of Antioquia holds works of Fernando Botero.
medina: Medina lies in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia. Its built-up area is surrounded by the Hejaz Mountains, empty valleys, agricultural land and old dormant volcanoes. Before Islam it was called Yathrib, a name attested in an inscription of the Babylonian king Nabonidus of the 6th century BCE and used in the Qur'an. According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad later renamed it Taybah or Tabah, and it came to be called Madinat an-Nabi, "City of the Prophet", and al-Madinah al-Munawwarah, "the Enlightened City", shortened to Madinah.

The city has been inhabited for about 1,500 years before the Hijrah, or about the 9th century BCE. By the fourth century Arab tribes were encroaching from Yemen, and around the time of Muhammad three prominent Jewish tribes lived there: the Banu Qaynuqa, the Banu Qurayza and the Banu Nadir.

Toward the end of the 5th century the Jewish rulers lost control of the city to the two Arab tribes, the 'Aws and Khazraj. In 622 Muhammad and an estimated 70 Meccan Muhajirun left Mecca over a few months for sanctuary in Yathrib. The longstanding enmity between the 'Aws and Khazraj was dampened as many of them and some local Jews embraced Islam, and Muhammad was agreed on as leader of the city. It served as the base of the early Muslim community, and a larger part of the Qur'an was revealed in Medina than in Mecca.

Later the city passed to the Umayyads, whose governors dug the spring called 'Ayn az-Zarqa'a and built irrigation ducts and dams, leading to an agricultural boom. It was held by the Mamluks of Egypt from 1254 to 1517 and then by the Ottomans, after Selim I conquered Mamluk Egypt.

In 1532 Suleiman built a fortress around it, and the Ottoman sultans repeatedly redesigned the Prophet's Mosque. The Sharif of Mecca, Husayn ibn Ali, attacked Medina on 6 June 1916, during the First World War, and the siege that followed brought food shortages, disease and mass emigration. The governor Fakhri Pasha held out until his own men arrested him and the Sharifate took the city on 10 January 1919. The Saudi forces conquered it on 5 December 1925.

Medina is the second holiest city in Islam after Mecca and the capital of Medina Province, with 1,477,023 inhabitants. Al-Masjid al-Nabawi, the Prophet's Mosque, was built by Muhammad in 622 and is the burial site of the prophet. The Quba Mosque is the oldest in Islam. The city also holds Masjid al-Qiblatayn, the Baqi' cemetery, Mount Uhud, site of the Battle of Uhud, and the King Fahd Glorious Qur'an Printing Complex.
mediterranean: The Mediterranean Sea is an intercontinental sea between Europe, Asia and Africa, almost completely enclosed by land. It connects to the Atlantic Ocean by the Strait of Gibraltar, only 14 km wide, to the Black Sea by the Bosporus, and to the Red Sea by the Suez Canal. It covers about 2,500,000 km2 and has fifteen marginal seas, among them the Aegean, Adriatic, Tyrrhenian and Marmara. Its average depth is 1,500 m, and the deepest point, 5,109 m, lies in the Calypso Deep in the Ionian Sea. The Nile is the longest river to end in it. Sicily and Sardinia are its two largest islands.

Geological evidence indicates that around 5.9 million years ago the sea was cut off from the Atlantic and was partly or completely dried up over some 600,000 years, in the Messinian salinity crisis. It was refilled about 5.3 million years ago by the Zanclean flood, in less than two years according to scientists' estimates.

The Levant, in the eastern Mediterranean, was among the first regions in the world with permanent human habitation, as early as 12,000 BCE. The earliest advanced civilisations on the sea were the Egyptians and the Minoans, who traded extensively with each other. Around 1200 BCE the Bronze Age Collapse destroyed many cities and trade routes in the east. The Greek city-states and the Phoenicians later colonised its coastlines extensively. Darius I of Persia, who conquered Egypt, built a canal linking the Red Sea to the Nile and so to the Mediterranean, wide enough for two triremes to pass and needing four days to traverse.

After the Punic Wars of the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE the Roman Republic defeated the Carthaginians and became the preeminent power in the western Mediterranean. Once Augustus founded the Roman Empire, the Romans called it Mare Nostrum, Our Sea. For the next 400 years the empire controlled the sea and virtually all its coasts from Gibraltar to the Levant, which earned it the nickname Roman Lake. Rome is the only state to have ever controlled all of its coasts.

The Romans also called the sea Mare Magnum and Mare Internum. The name Mare Mediterraneum, meaning in the middle of land, is first attested in the 6th century in the work of Isidore of Seville. Arabic writers called it the Sea of the Romans, and the Ancient Egyptians called it Wadj-wr, great green. The countries on its shores include Spain, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt and Morocco, and Cyprus and Malta are island countries within it. Its mild winters and warm summers give their name to the Mediterranean climate type.
megali-idea: The expression first appeared in the debates between Prime Minister Ioannis Kolettis and King Otto that preceded the constitution of 1844, but the hope behind it was older. Greeks had long looked for liberation from Ottoman rule and a restoration of the Byzantine Empire; folklore told that the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, had been turned to marble and lay beneath the Golden Gate of Constantinople awaiting the call to reconquer the city. The state created in 1830 was designed by the Great Powers, and most ethnic Greeks still lived outside it, within the Ottoman Empire.

The new state was imagined as the Greece of Two Continents and Five Seas, reaching from the Ionian Sea to Anatolia and the Black Sea and from Thrace, Macedonia and Epirus to Crete and Cyprus. When the Danish prince Wilhelm Georg was elected king in 1863 he was styled King of the Hellenes rather than King of Greece, implying a king of all Greeks wherever they lived.

The Ionian Islands were acquired in 1864. In 1897, with violence growing in Crete, a Greek force of 1,500 men under Colonel Timoleon Vassos landed at Kolymbari on 1 February and proclaimed the island's union with Greece. Irregulars then raided Turkish outposts in Thessaly without orders, and the Ottoman Empire declared war. The Greek army fell back, an armistice was signed in May, and Greece lost small border territories and paid reparations; Crete became an autonomous state with Prince George of Greece as High Commissioner.

Eleftherios Venizelos, a Cretan who became prime minister after the Goudi coup of 1909, was a major proponent of the idea, and under him Greek territory doubled in the Balkan Wars of 1912–13. Greece joined the Allies in 1917 and afterwards gained a protectorate over Smyrna and its hinterland, where a referendum was to follow five years of Greek administration, and a frontier in Thrace a few miles from the walls of Constantinople.

Turkish revolutionaries defeated the Greek army and expelled the Greeks from Anatolia. By the Treaty of Lausanne, Greece ceded Eastern Thrace, Imbros, Tenedos and Smyrna. During the conflict 151,892 Greeks had already fled Asia Minor; the treaty moved 1,104,216 Greeks from Turkey, while 380,000 Turks left Greece. The League of Nations arranged a loan of 150 million francs to help settle the refugees. In 1930 Venizelos paid an official visit to Turkey, where he proposed Mustafa Kemal for the Nobel Peace Prize. The Dodecanese were acquired after the Second World War, in 1947.
melbourne: Melbourne occupies much of the northern and eastern coastlines of Port Phillip Bay, in the southeastern part of mainland Australia. The Boonwurrung and Woiwurrung languages call the area Narrm or Naarm; in Boonwurrung, Naarm means the Bay. The city is named after William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne, who was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom when it was founded in 1835. At its centre is the Hoddle Grid, a grid of streets measuring about 1.61 by 0.80 kilometres, whose southern edge fronts onto the Yarra River.

Aboriginal Australians have lived in the Melbourne area for at least 40,000 years. When British colonists arrived in the 19th century, up to 20,000 Kulin people from three language groups, the Wurundjeri, Bunurong and Wathaurong, lived there. The area was an important meeting place for the clans of the Kulin nation alliance and a vital source of food and water. A short-lived British penal settlement was founded at Port Phillip in 1803, then part of the Colony of New South Wales. Melbourne itself was founded in 1835 with the arrival of free settlers from Van Diemen's Land, now Tasmania, and was incorporated as a Crown settlement in 1837.

Queen Victoria declared it a city in 1847, and in 1851 it became the capital of the newly separated Colony of Victoria. The Victorian gold rush of the 1850s began a long boom which, by the late 1880s, had made it one of the largest and wealthiest cities in Australia and the world. After the federation of Australia in 1901 it was the interim seat of government until Canberra became the permanent capital in 1927. In 1956 it hosted the Summer Olympics, the first Olympic Games held outside Europe and the United States.

Melbourne is the capital of the state of Victoria and the second most populous city in Australia, with more than five million people. It is known for the Victorian architecture left by the gold rush and the land boom of the 1880s; the Royal Exhibition Building, completed in 1880, is World Heritage listed. Little survives from before the gold rush, St James Old Cathedral (1839) and St Francis' Church (1845) being among the few examples in the city centre.

The city gave rise to Australian rules football, Australian impressionism and Australian cinema. The Melbourne Cup horse race, first held in 1861, was declared a public holiday for all Melburnians in 1873. The University of Melbourne is the second-oldest university in Australia.
melilla: Melilla lies in northwest Africa on the shores of the Alboran Sea, on the eastern side of the peninsula of Cape Tres Forcas, at the foot of Mount Gurugú and around the mouth of the intermittent stream called the Río de Oro. The city is arranged in a wide semicircle around the beach and the port. Its urban nucleus was originally a fortress, Melilla la Vieja, built on a peninsular mound about 30 m high. The Moroccan settlement of Beni Ansar lies immediately to the south.

Melilla was a Phoenician and later Punic trading establishment under the name Rusadir, taken from the Phoenician name of the nearby Cape Three Forks. After Carthage's defeat in the Punic Wars it fell under the Roman client state of Mauretania, and it was later part of the province of Mauretania Tingitana. It was made a Roman colony in 46 CE.

In the 15th century the city declined, like most Mediterranean cities of the Kingdom of Fez, as Atlantic ports eclipsed them. After the Catholic Monarchs conquered the Kingdom of Granada in 1492, their secretary Hernando de Zafra gathered information on the North African coast, and he reported that in 1494 the locals had expelled the authority of the Sultan of Fez and offered to pledge loyalty. The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 placed Melilla within the sphere of Castile, but the conquest waited. It was seized by Christians in 1497 and was a condominium of the House of Medina Sidonia and the Crown of Castile until 1556.

For much of the early modern period the fortress of Melilla la Vieja remained a military garrison with a small civilian population. The current limits of Spanish territory around it were fixed by treaties with Morocco in 1859, 1860, 1861 and 1894, and the area between the old fortress and the outer forts was settled by mainland Spaniards, Sephardi Jews and Riffians.

Melilla became an autonomous city in 1995, having until then been a municipality of Málaga. Spanish is the official language and Tarifit, the Berber language of the Rif, is also spoken. The Chapel of Santiago, with a dome of the mid-16th century, is a rare example of Gothic architecture in Africa, and the architect Enrique Nieto left the city the second largest concentration of Modernista works in Spain after Barcelona.
mesopotamia: Mesopotamia lies within the Tigris–Euphrates river system, in the northern part of the Fertile Crescent, and corresponds roughly to the territory of modern Iraq. In the broader sense it also includes parts of present-day southwestern Iran, southeastern Turkey, northeastern Syria and Kuwait. The climate is semi-arid, with a vast desert expanse in the north that gives way in the south to a region of marshes, lagoons, mudflats and reed banks of about 15,000 square kilometres. In the south the two rivers unite and empty into the Persian Gulf. The name comes from the Greek for land between rivers.

Mesopotamia is the site of the earliest developments of the Neolithic Revolution, from around 10,000 BCE. Writing emerged there in a pictographic script, proto-cuneiform, in the Uruk IV period, in the late 4th millennium BCE, and the documented record of events begins in the early third millennium BCE with cuneiform records of early dynastic kings. The Sumerians and Akkadians dominated the region from the beginning of recorded history, around 3100 BCE, to the fall of Babylon in 539 BCE. The rise of empires began with Sargon of Akkad around 2350 BCE.

In the early second millennium BCE Mesopotamian society divided into Assyria in the north and Babylonia in the south. From 900 to 612 BCE the Neo-Assyrian Empire controlled much of the ancient Near East. The Babylonians, long overshadowed by Assyria, then seized power and dominated the region for a century as the final independent Mesopotamian realm until the modern era. In 539 BCE Cyrus the Great conquered Mesopotamia for the Achaemenid Empire, and Alexander the Great took it in 332 BCE; among his successors the Seleucids emerged victorious.

Around 150 BCE the region was under the Parthian Empire and became a battleground between Romans and Parthians. In 226 CE the eastern regions fell to the Sassanid Persians under Ardashir I, and the division of the region between the Roman and Sassanid empires lasted until the Muslim conquest of the 7th century CE, after which it came to be known as Iraq.

The earliest language written in Mesopotamia was Sumerian. Akkadian became dominant under the Akkadian and Assyrian empires, but Sumerian was kept for administrative, religious, literary and scientific purposes. Mesopotamian mathematics used a base-60 numeral system, the source of the 60-minute hour and the 360-degree circle, and Babylonian astronomers could predict eclipses and solstices.

Mesopotamia corresponds roughly to modern Iraq. Modern Assyrians remain descendants of the native Mesopotamians, and the Marsh Iraqis are genetically and culturally the closest modern people to the ancient Sumerians.
messina: Messina stands in the north-eastern corner of Sicily, on the western shore of the Strait of Messina, and is an important access point to Calabria on the mainland, at Villa San Giovanni and Reggio Calabria. Its municipal area of about 213.75 square kilometres stretches along 56 kilometres of coast, which makes it the longest and most maritime city in Italy. The climate is subtropical Mediterranean, with long hot summers and a wet, mild winter.

The early name of the city was Zancle, which Thucydides derived from a Siculian word meaning scythe, because of the shape of its natural harbour. At the beginning of the 5th century BCE Anaxilas of Rhegium settled refugees from Messenia there and renamed it Messene. It was Messana in the Roman age and became Messina in the Byzantine period. It was a major Roman city, contracted under Byzantine and Arab rule, and rose sharply in importance in the Norman era. Between the late Middle Ages and the mid-17th century it competed with Palermo to be the capital of the Kingdom of Sicily.

After an anti-Spanish revolt Messina was put to fire and sword in 1678, and its ruling class was annihilated. An earthquake seriously damaged it in 1783, and in 1908 another destroyed it almost entirely and killed about half the population. Rebuilding began in 1912, largely in the Liberty style. Allied bombers heavily attacked the city in 1943 during the landing in Sicily, in some 2,800 air raids, and it received the Gold Medal of Military Valor.

Messina is the capital of its metropolitan city and the third largest city on Sicily. Its port, for thousands of years one of the main commercial crossroads of the Mediterranean, is the first in Italy by number of passengers in transit, with ferries to Villa San Giovanni. The University of Messina was founded in 1548 by Pope Paul III, and the city has been an archdiocese since the same year. The Museo Regionale holds paintings by Caravaggio and by the Renaissance painter Antonello da Messina. The Good Friday procession of the Barette goes back to 1610.
mexico: Mexico covers 1,972,550 square kilometres, the thirteenth-largest country in the world, with coastlines on the Pacific Ocean, the Gulf of California, the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea. The central and northern territories lie at high altitudes. The highest elevations are in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, which includes Pico de Orizaba at 5,700 metres and Popocatépetl at 5,462 metres, and the Sierra Madre Oriental and Sierra Madre Occidental cross the country from north to south. The Chicxulub crater lies on the Yucatán peninsula, and much of the land mass is unsuited to agriculture because of aridity, soil or terrain.

Human presence dates back to at least 11,500 BCE, although dates as old as 28,000 BCE have been proposed for less securely dated sites. Mexico is the site of the domestication of maize, tomato and beans, which allowed sedentary agricultural villages to begin around 5000 BCE.
